utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to say good morning to the interpreters and to make sure that they understand what I am saying. They can hear me. Good morning. Good morning, everybody. Very well. Let me say good morning to the Defence and to the Prosecution counsel and to the accused, and I believe that we can now continue. Mr. Hayman, the floor is yours. I think you said you had about an hour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I expect about another hour, and then we would commence with our first witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The time is yours, of course; you do with it what you like. We will squeeze a little harder with the witnesses, but for the opening statement, the time is yours, and you can use it as you like. Please proceed, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you for your patience. I know my remarks are lengthy. Before I begin, let me note that, as I said yesterday, the relief model is made to scale, but the height, such as the height of the mountains, has been magnified by a factor of three, so it is actually 3-1 in terms of height, which was done for readability, but if the mountains were actually made to scale, in other words, they would only be one-third the height that they are depicted on the model. I wanted to stress that for clarity, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. Yes, we did really have impressions here that this was more like the Alps than it would be Central Bosnia, but thank you for your specifications. But this also allows us, the Judges, not to have to come down to look at the model. Thank you for your explanations. It will be noted in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. When we broke yesterday, we had discussed the 16th and 17th of April, 1993, and those events, and now I would like to turn to two other events that occurred during the heavy and chaotic fighting from the 15th to the 19th of April, 1993, in the Lasva Valley. On the 18th of April, Vitez was rocked by a huge explosion that occurred within Stari Vitez. The Operative Zone headquarters, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, had no prior knowledge that an explosion would occur. The explosion occurred behind BH army lines and was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hayman. I'm trying to follow your organisation. You are using a written document. I'm trying to follow what you are saying, but you are still talking about the fighting at this point; is that correct? I noted it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The subject, Mr. President, is the war in Vitez and the Lasva Valley the latter half of April, is where I am now, in terms of the chronology. I have discussed the fighting that began between the 16th and 20th, actually, in the different villages around Vitez, culminating with the fight in Gacice on the 20th, but now I am going back to discuss two other events that occurred during this time period, the truck bomb on the 18th of April and then I will turn to the shelling of Zenica in the marketplace on the 19th, the following day. On the 18th, Vitez was rocked by this explosion. The explosion was caused by a truck bomb planned and instigated by Darko Kraljevic, commander of the Vitezovi unit. It was organised without the knowledge of Tihomir Blaskic. When he heard the explosion, he was surprised, and he directed the headquarters staff to find out what had occurred. The reports he was given will be presented to Your Honours. There was no conclusive information provided to him concerning this bomb. The following day, on the 19th of April, several artillery shells hit the marketplace in Central Zenica, killing and wounding a large number of civilians. Without artillery radar at the time, it is not possible to identify with precision the origin of those shells. The evidence will show that from April until into June 1993, Zenica was regularly shelled by the Bosnian Serbs from the Vlassic feature and/or from other locations north of Travnik. Tihomir Blaskic did not order the shelling of Zenica on the 19th of April or at any other time. On the 19th of April, he had no reason to believe that Zenica would be shelled by the HVO or by anyone else. After the word of the shelling spread to BRITBAT, Colonel Stewart visited Tihomir Blaskic and told him that Zenica had been shelled by 155-millimetre artillery. The HVO did not have a 155-millimetre artillery piece in Central Bosnia. Tihomir Blaskic asked Colonel Stewart to investigate with him and to visit HVO artillery sites and to go to Zenica so that the HVO investigators could visit the scene of the shell impacts. Colonel Stewart declined the request on the ground that Zenica was too dangerous for HVO personnel to visit. As I have discussed, in mid-April, Tihomir Blaskic issued numerous directives to HVO units not to target civilians but, rather, to protect them in times of war activity. Although after mid-April the Serbs regularly shelled Zenica, there is no allegation in the indictment that the HVO did so. Tihomir Blaskic is also charged with responsibility for the unlawful detention of Bosnian Muslim civilians and the inhumane treatment of such persons. The evidence will show that on the morning of the 16th of April, he did not order the detention of any civilians. Rather, when a general conflict on the territory of the Vitez municipality occurred, large numbers of civilians were detained by local units. They appear to have been motivated in part by fears of attacks from the Muslim population, by fears concerning the fate of some 20.000 Croats in Zenica at the time, and their continued detention may have been motivated by the prospect of private exchanges organised for a fee. The fear and panic that caused civilians to be detained was mirrored in Zenica where, on the same day, large numbers of Croat civilians were being detained. What did Tihomir Blaskic do with respect to this activity? He tried repeatedly to prevent the detaining of civilians and to protect those that had been detained. On the 18th of April, he ordered all HVO units to exchange detained soldiers and civilians at once. On the 21st of April, he ordered all units to protect civilians caught up in combat and to provide humane treatment to all detained civilians. Again, after further combat activity in the summer, on the 17th of June, he ordered, reminded all HVO units to prevent the arrest of civilians during combat activities or the taking of hostages. In the chaotic atmosphere that prevailed in Central Bosnia, the most effective way to get detained civilians released was to organise rapid exchanges. This was principally a civilian matter, and by the agreement of all concerned, Commissions for Exchange were set up in Vitez and Zenica, headed by civil authorities. At the same time, Tihomir Blaskic did order all HVO personnel to fully cooperate with the International Red Cross and others to facilitate such exchanges. But when his orders to release all detainees clashed with the preferences of local civil authorities, the civil authorities did as they pleased, and the evidence will so demonstrate. We will also introduce evidence in our case concerning his efforts to calm rather than to inflame the situation with respect to the plight of Croats in Zenica during the April 1993 conflict. For example, when large numbers of displaced Croats wished to return to Zenica after the worst of the conflict there had subsided, he supported their decision and assisted them in returning to their homes in the Zenica municipality. The evidence will also show that at the height of the conflict in mid-April, his concerns about the safety of Croats in Zenica were genuine and were fully justified. From the 16th of April on in Zenica, Bosnian Croats were victimised in large numbers. They were murdered, beaten, detained, their houses were looted, and hundreds of their homes were burned. Due to this atmosphere, and for other reasons I will discuss in a few minutes, approximately 9.000 Croats fled the Zenica municipality between April and the end of 1993. Those who stayed continued, unfortunately, to be harassed, and many of the men, Bosnian Croat males, who stayed in Zenica, were forcibly conscripted and sent to the very first positions on the frontline with the Bosnian Serbs. Their treatment is reflected by the fact that after the Washington Agreement in 1994, another 5.000 Bosnian Croats chose to leave the Zenica municipality. Now I would like to return to the Kiseljak municipality where there is one unlawful attack on civilians charged relating to Rotilj in April of 1993, that is, during that time period. The evidence will show there was no order from the Operative Zone headquarters to attack Rotilj. What did happen in Rotilj on the 18th of April? Local HVO soldiers did go to Rotilj on that day. They went to the village and told the BH army commander - there was a BH army or Territorial Defence unit in Rotilj - and told him that they had been directed to disarm the TO unit in the village. They asked for his cooperation. They sat down on the front porch of a home in the village and had coffee and discussed the problem. But the BH commander would not agree. He was not in a position, for whatever reason, to agree to disarm and, predictably, a conflict started. While searching homes in the village for weapons, one HVO soldier was apparently shot and killed by refugees, Muslim refugees who were housed in the village at that time. Repeating a pattern I have alluded to earlier, some of the soldiers at the scene took immediate revenge, killing several of the civilians, Muslim civilians, and burning six or eight homes, however many it was. This was not activity directed or condoned by the Operative Zone headquarters, nor was it reported to it. In fact, it was contrary to all orders issued by the Operative Zone headquarters and Tihomir Blaskic. We will also prove, Your Honours, that Rotilj was not a prison camp. After the incident I described, the local HVO commander made a decision to erect a checkpoint on the main road to Rotilj and gave instructions that no one was to pass into Rotilj without his permission. He did this for the protection of the residents. There were many roads and paths leading out of Rotilj, some of which led directly to BH army territory near Fojnica. The residents were free to leave, but Croat refugees and some criminals who wanted to take revenge on the Muslim residents of Rotilj were kept out by this checkpoint. The same food and aid was delivered to Rotilj as was provided to Croats in need in the Kiseljak municipality. In fact, no distinctions based on national groups were made in the distribution of aid. In the summer and fall of 1993, there was good reason to take steps to protect Muslim residents in the Kiseljak municipality. That municipality became increasingly lawless as the security situation deteriorated. When Travnik fell, that is, when Travnik was taken over by the BH army in June 1993, large numbers of displaced HVO soldiers came to Kiseljak from Travnik through Serb territory. On the 3rd of July, '93, two days after General Morillon declared Fojnica an oasis of peace, the BH army attacked the HVO in the town and drove them out. Of the 7.000 Croat residents of Fojnica, all but 150 fled, and they fled to Kiseljak. Their homes were looted and, over time, burned by angry persons, angry refugees, perhaps angry BH army soldiers in a pattern, this Court will see, that was repeated in other locations. These throngs of displaced persons and soldiers arriving in Kiseljak were joined by others later in 1993 when the BH army overran, first, Kakanj and then Vares. Literally, tens of thousands of refugees and displaced soldiers arrived in Kiseljak. Security was so poor in Kiseljak that even in 1994, after the Washington Agreement, EC monitors visiting the municipality were afraid to get out of their cars. There were incidents in Kiseljak during this period directed against both Muslim residents and Muslim places of worship. The evidence will show that Tihomir Blaskic could not, despite diligent efforts, exercise effective control over HVO in the Kiseljak enclave. As I have said, the Vitez-Busovaca enclave was encircled by the BH army and BH army territory. By contrast, the Kiseljak enclave bordered on a stretch of Bosnian Serb controlled territory, and that's reflected in some of the maps, I believe, that we were looking at yesterday. For a price, transportation of goods and people between the Kiseljak enclave and Herzegovina was possible travelling through Bosnian Serb territory. So a situation developed in which Tihomir Blaskic in Vitez was cut off and isolated, but the Kiseljak enclave had a connection to Herzegovina, to the HVO main command in Mostar. The Kiseljak HVO's superior access to the HVO main command in Mostar dictated the actual command relationships that evolved in 1993 between those three entities, the HVO main command, the 3rd Operative Zone for Central Bosnia, and the HVO units commanded by the HVO commander in Kiseljak, which included not only the Ban Jelacic brigade, but also the brigades in Vares and in Kakanj and a unit in Fojnica. Again, through Serb territory, the HVO commander in Kiseljak could travel to Vares and Kakanj and, in fact, did travel to Vares and had effective control over HVO units in those locations. The HVO commander in Kiseljak was Ivica Rajic. In January 1993, he was replaced by another officer, and you'll hear about that, but by May of '93, he was back in power in Kiseljak. According to Rajic, and I quote -- could we have the next slide, please. This is a quote from the HVO commander in Kiseljak. "In the beginning, Blaskic was my superior, but later he was transferred to Vitez, while I remained in Kiseljak. Although Blaskic was formally my superior even then, the conditions on the ground imposed a situation where he and I were equally responsible to the main staff of the HVO, he for his sector and I for mine." This proposition will be confirmed by other documentary evidence. In August 1993, General Petkovic of the main HVO command in Mostar issued a simultaneous directive to Tihomir Blaskic and Ivica Rajic to coordinate on certain operative matters. In other words, the commander up here issued a directive, the same piece of paper, to both the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia and to the HVO commander in Kiseljak, supposedly subordinate to the 3rd Operative Zone, to coordinate. That would be normal if those subordinate entities were on the same level, such as if Rajic had been the commander of the 1st Operative Zone, wherever that was, in Mostar or some other location, but, of course, he wasn't. He was the commander of a unit who was supposed to be subordinate to Tihomir Blaskic. Similarly, the liaison officer at the HVO Kiseljak brigade reported directly to the HVO command in Mostar, not to the Operative Zone headquarters in Vitez. The liaison officer was the principal person to whom complaints and concerns about war activities were raised by international organisations. The inability of Tihomir Blaskic to control Ivica Rajic was a source of concern to him. He tried to control Rajic. He continued to issue orders to Rajic during 1993, but he was not able to control him, both due to his physical isolation and due to the superior contacts between the Kiseljak HVO and the HVO main command in Mostar. Approximately half of the specific charges in the indictment pertain to events in the Kiseljak enclave after it was cut off from the Operative Zone headquarters in Vitez in April of 1993. Now I'd like to return to the Vitez enclave and briefly discuss the balance of the war in that enclave after the 20th of April, 1993. From the 16th of April onwards, the war in the Vitez-Busovaca enclave was, from the perspective of the HVO, a war for the survival of the HVO and the Croat residents of the Lasva Valley. They were completely encircled and outnumbered by the BH army by as many as ten to one. There were persistent shortages of all supplies, as well as basic necessities of life. Water and power were periodically cut off by the BH army which controlled both. The only available hospital was a makeshift facility in the Nova Bila church. Mortaring and sniping of soldiers and the civilian population was an everyday occurrence from BH army positions. Their situation continued to deteriorate over 1993. In the January conflict, 65 per cent of the Busovaca municipality had been lost. That is, the BH army had taken control over it. In mid April, Kuber Mountain was lost, as were the HVO brigade and approximately 20 Croat villages in the Zenica municipality. In the first half of June, Travnik was lost. By the 12th of June, half of the Novi Travnik municipality was lost, again, to the BH army. On the 12th of June, Kakanj fell to the BH army. In July, Fojnica fell to the BH army. In September, the dominant feature at Zaberje south of the main supply route in the Vitez-Busovaca enclave fell. In December, Krizansevo Selo fell with 75 dead, and in January, Buhina Kuce fell also. After April 1993, there is one unlawful attack on civilians charged in the indictment in the Vitez or Busovaca municipalities. That is an attack alleged on Vitez in August of 1993. Perhaps it's a reference to an attack that did occur in Stari Vitez the prior month. The Defence doesn't know, after 15 months in trial, what this relates to. There are two alleged acts of unlawful destruction of property in the Vitez or Busovaca municipalities after April of 1993. They pertain to Stari Vitez and Grbavica. I will discuss each briefly in turn. There was an attack on Stari Vitez on the 18th of July, 1993. It was planned and instigated by Darko Kraljevic in retaliation for an attack by the BH army on his brother a day or two before. Tihomir Blaskic did not plan or approve this attack. His lack of involvement in the attack is reflected by the fact that it was an amateurish attempt and that a large number of Vitezovi soldiers were killed while attempting to approach Stari Vitez. The Court will be in a position to compare, for example, that operation with operations that the Operative Zone headquarters did approve and participate in the planning of, such as the Grbavica operation, which I will discuss in a moment. There were many proposals to attack Stari Vitez in the summer and fall of 1993 as the HVO military position deteriorated. Stari Vitez was a drain on HVO resources. Constant mortaring and sniping claimed civilian lives and soldiers' lives in Vitez, and as that occurred, demands to do something about Stari Vitez escalated within the HVO and in the Croat community. Tihomir Blaskic, however, consistently rejected proposals to attack Stari Vitez on the grounds that too many civilian casualties within Stari Vitez would result. The only other post-April 1993 unlawful attack on civilian property alleged in the indictment relates to Grbavica. Grbavica is located here to the northwest of Vitez and was a dominant hill feature immediately adjacent to the BRITBAT base which was located here. There was a BH unit in Grbavica, part of the 325th Mountain Brigade. One objective of that unit was to close down the main supply route, this part of the supply route which ran from Vitez and into Travnik and, if you took the fork, to Novi Travnik, to close it to HVO and Croat civilian traffic, and that it did. Through sniper positions on the hill, the Grbavica hill, the BH army was able to effectively close the main supply route and force the HVO for many, many months to use an unimproved track, a dirt track, which went back some distance below the main supply road, which, of course, was a paved or sealed road, a much better road. They used that dirt track in order to avoid the problem, rather than to confront it directly. You can see from the hill feature that it is, literally, the only hill feature to the north of the road in the immediate area, and it was the dominant feature. There were many civilian and military casualties from this hill feature, and it grew to a head in late August or September 1993 when several school children were shot by snipers on Grbavica while returning home from church on a Sunday. The HVO responded to these murders with the approval of Tihomir Blaskic, who felt it was his responsibility to do something to protect innocent lives that were being lost due to the sniper positions on Grbavica. On the 7th of September, the HVO launched a military action against the BH army positions on Grbavica. A battle ensued that spanned, approximately, two days. It was a well-planned, well-executed military action. Despite the fact that there were civilian residents of the village, there were either no or virtually no, there may have been one, civilian casualties in the course of those two days of fighting. Unlike the Ahmici attack on the 16th or the Stari Vitez assault in July, this action against the Grbavica BH army snipers in military positions was approved by the Operative Zone headquarters. The evidence will show it was a proper military action. After the attack was over, the BH army had withdrawn, and the frontline moved forward to a new location. Sometime after the battle was over, scavengers started to arrive in Grbavica. Individual and private looting occurred in which scavengers, for example, stripped the wood off of houses to use for firewood, such as the window frames. Desperate people, desperate times, Your Honours. Looting or burning portions of Grbavica after the military conflict had concluded was not directed or sanctioned by the Operative Zone headquarters in any way. Any HVO soldiers who engaged in such conduct did so contrary to express orders from Tihomir Blaskic, and those orders were issued prior to the Grbavica operation. After the mid April conflict, if I could have the next slide, please, Tihomir Blaskic issued the following order on the 22nd of April, 1993. It's not a coincidence that this is the day or at about this time that he was apprised of the nature of the massacre and the burning of homes in Ahmici. He ordered on the 22nd, and I quote: "In order to prevent incidents in which houses and other commercial facilities are set on fire and looted, I hereby issue the following order: 1) I strictly prohibit the torching of houses and other commercial facilities and looting in the zone of responsibility of the command of the Central Bosnia Operations Zone controlled by HVO units. The most stringent measures shall be taken against violators of this order pursuant to the regulation book on military discipline in HVO units." He had issued a second specific order, this order on the 19th of June, 1993, again, to HVO units, forbidding the lighting of houses or other objects on fire or the theft of property, and he warned those units that such conduct would be punished through military discipline and the military courts. Thus, prior to Grbavica, Tihomir Blaskic issued at least two specific orders directed to the type of conduct which is alleged to have occurred in the indictment. The Grbavica incident, that is, following the battle, was the first and last of its kind charged in the indictment in the Vitez-Busovaca enclave following the mid April 1993 conflict. What else is alleged to have occurred after the April 1993 conflict in the Vitez-Busovaca enclave? There are no specific acts of unlawful destruction of sacral objects after April 1993 in the Vitez-Busovaca enclave. There are charges of such acts in 1993 with no month specified in the indictment with respect to Busovaca and Stari Vitez. If the allegation as to Stari Vitez refers to damage due to the truck bomb, then I have already discussed it. If the allegation pertains to the firing of rifle or anti-aircraft fire at the mosque in Stari Vitez at some other time in 1993, the evidence will show that damage to the mosque from such fire was minor and was the result of a single incident, not a plan or an operation directed from or acquiesced by the Operative Zone headquarters. The fact is, the HVO could have destroyed the mosque in Stari Vitez by fire, artillery fire, or what have you at any time. It never did so, and the fact that it did not do so was consistent with the orders and directives of Tihomir Blaskic on that subject. For example, on the 19th of June, he directed that special protection, this was a direction to all HVO units, and I quote: "Special protection is to be provided for sacral objects." The order specifically lists mosques and other religious sites as locations to be afforded special protection. What did he do when he learned of damage to religious sites by suspected HVO perpetrators? If I could have the next slide, please. He reacted strongly. That's what he did. On the 17th of August, he issued the following order to the commander of the Kiseljak brigade. Again, this was Ivica Rajic, who we were discussing earlier, who is in a different enclave from the Vitez-Busovaca enclave, an enclave connected through Serb territory with the HVO main command in Mostar. What did that order say? I quote: "On 17 August 1993, we learned that a religious building in Kiseljak had been demolished. In order to establish the facts and conduct an investigation, I hereby order: 1) Send a precise report about the demolition of the religious building. 2) What have you done to start an investigation and find the perpetrator? 3) What have you found out and what will be your next steps in this case?" The religious building that was the subject of this order was a Muslim site. Now I would like to address briefly the siege of Stari Vitez. BH army units in Stari Vitez were blocked by the HVO from mid April on, and frontlines developed between the two involving bunkers and trenches and the like. These lines did not move during the balance of the war. As I have said, Stari Vitez as well as Kruscica were points from which sniper and other fire were routinely directed at the HVO and civilians in Vitez. The HVO sought to contain these units and to prevent any breakout action from them. Tihomir Blaskic never directed an attack on Stari Vitez. His contact with Stari Vitez was limited to the fact that his headquarters, the Hotel Vitez, was under intermittent sniper fire from BH army positions in Stari Vitez. He never went into Stari Vitez during the war. If he had, he would have been almost certainly killed. There were, as one would expect, exchanges of various forms of fire on the frontline around Stari Vitez. Those exchanges were of a local nature. There were casualties in both Stari Vitez and Vitez as a result of those exchanges. The entire population of Stari Vitez was mobilised by the BH army. Women bore arms in Stari Vitez, and in those circumstances, soldiers and civilians in the able-bodied population became virtually indistinguishable. When there were casualties in Stari Vitez, they were invariably presented to UNPROFOR as civilians by Sefkija Dzidic. It was a shrewd and successful propaganda effort. Where a warring party deliberately blurs military and civilian objects, an attacking commander cannot be blamed for collateral civilian consequences and casualties. The BH army in Stari Vitez mixed and collocated civilian and military sites. Private cellars and homes were used to house munitions and military supplies. Military installations were unmarked in order to reduce the likelihood that they would be targeted. In other words, there was a deliberate blending of military and civilian objects in Stari Vitez. Tihomir Blaskic promoted the delivery of aid into Stari Vitez as well as free access for relief organisations in areas under HVO control, which included the perimeter of Stari Vitez and the southern perimeter of Kruscica. We will introduce his many directives on that subject, and there were many. He promoted the evacuation of the wounded and he declined suggestions, as I have said, for an attack on Stari Vitez. Repeated offers were made for civilians to temporarily leave Stari Vitez, if they wished. But keeping aid routes open into Stari Vitez and Kruscica was not fully within the control of Tihomir Blaskic. Angry and hungry civilians posed a threat to relieve convoys throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to return briefly, Mr. President, to the issue of population movements during the war. There were dramatic population movements in Central Bosnia during the war. In fact, far more Bosnian Croats were displaced as a result of the war than were Bosnian Muslims, although that is not of particular relevance. An important issue for this Court will be: Why did these movements occur? The evidence will show several important facts on this topic. First, Tihomir Blaskic never directed the forcible movement of civilians from their homes. Never. Second, civilians requesting, wishing to relocate, was a subject that was principally a civilian matter. Tihomir Blaskic was concerned with the defence of the enclaves of Central Bosnia, principally the Vitez-Busovaca enclave after he was isolated, and with protecting the enclaves against BH army units within their borders. He had no interest in the movement of civilian populations. What was his position on civilian movements? Because movements sometimes involved frontline crossings, he was called upon from time to time to address that issue. Could a group of civilians cross a military boundary, a military frontline? He had one position on this issue: freedom of movement. He had the same position, he had this position, prior to April 1993, when tens of thousands of Muslim refugees and displaced persons migrated into the Lasva Valley. He had the same position after April when many of those same persons wished to leave. He had the same position with respect to Croats and Muslims. When thousands of Croats wished to return to Zenica, at least hundreds -- I don't have a number for the Court at this time -- in late April, he approved and facilitated their crossing the frontlines to return to Zenica. Why did these ethnic populations tend to move during the civil war? The same question applies to both Croat and Muslim displaced persons. To be sure, there were persons driven from one place to another by violent acts. That certainly occurred in Ahmici when people fled for their lives, it occurred in Dusina, it occurred in Miletici, and there were persons whose homes were destroyed either as a result of combat operations or for no legitimate purpose whatsoever, and hence they had no home to return to. Although less dramatic, the evidence will show there are far more important reasons that explain these large population movements, at least four reasons. First, many persons moved prior to the outbreak of open war in a particular area in order to avoid exposure to the fighting. Second, many persons moved when war or active fighting broke out in their area. They moved to get out of a war zone. An example here would be in Grbavica when, after the military operation there began, UNPROFOR evacuated the civilian population at some point during the battle. There is nothing wrong with that, it's normal, and lives may have been saved. A third reason for these movements was when the HVO or the BH army exerted control over a particular area, many persons wished to relocate to an area under the control of their national army. Again, that is neither good nor bad, but it was a fact, and we will so demonstrate. Fourthly, many of these movements were due to the fact that when able-bodied men, soldiers, were detained, such as in Zenica and Vitez, and then were exchanged, frequently their families wished to move with them and did. What did Tihomir Blaskic do to try and ensure freedom of movement for civilians so that no one was forced to leave their homes? He never targeted civilians or civilian objects for any military action. He repeatedly ordered HVO soldiers to protect, that is, HVO subordinate commanders, to order their soldiers to protect civilians and civilian homes during combat operations. He did his best to ensure public security and order for all citizens, and he specifically ordered that persons not be expelled from their homes, and I would like to show the Court one of these orders. If I could have the next slide, please? On the 24th of April, 1993, he directed that the military police and the civil police should work together to the following end. Mr. President, this is a longer quote. There is a written French translation of this quote which, although it won't be on the screen, you should have it in the materials you have before you. I quote from the order of Tihomir Blaskic of 24 April, 1993: "Because a large number of flats temporarily vacant which are being forced into by persons carrying arms -- soldiers of the Croatian Defence Force and other persons -- and in order to enforce public order and peace in the town of Vitez as well as to prevent such negative developments, I ORDER: Unlawful taking of the flats and stealing of property from the flats which belong to citizens who, for different reasons, are temporarily not present, is to be prevented by all means, including by use of force ..." He gave this task principally to the 4th Battalion of the military police, although he asked that the civil police work together to implement this goal. With thousands of displaced persons and high emotions in the enclaves of Central Bosnia, this was a difficult order to enforce. There were also criminal elements within the HVO to be dealt with. But Tihomir Blaskic did not give up. When he learned that his orders were not being effectively implemented, what did he do? Could I have the next slide, please? The earlier order, as I said, was issued to the military police of the HVO. In May, the end of May, the 31st, 1993, he issued the following extraordinary order, and I quote. Again, there is a French translation in hard copy, Mr. President, of this order, of this passage from the order. The order in its entirety will be presented to Your Honours in our case. "On 30 May, 1993, the officer on duty in the Operative Zone Central Bosnia informed me that Mr. Fringe Ramljak and Mr. Slavko Hrgic, both members of the military police, were expelling Muslim families by force. This was despite the order which bans such actions and for which the above-named gentlemen are responsible." A reference to his prior order directing the military police to ensure that Muslim families are not expelled from their homes and their property is not looted. I continue quoting this passage: "In order to prevent further actions that hinder the execution of orders and the correct behaviour of Military Police members carrying out their assignments, I HEREBY ORDER: 1. Conduct an investigation into this case and take disciplinary measures against the culprits in this incident. 2. Report to me explaining why, despite a number of warnings, certain members of your unit --" Again a reference to the military police unit. " -- are still causing such negative occurrences instead of protecting public order, and suggest further actions to prevent such occurrences in the future." Tihomir Blaskic himself never took an apartment in Vitez. He had no apartment in Vitez. He felt there were many others who needed one more than he. He lived in a small room in the Hotel Vitez throughout the war. The last topic I will address, Your Honours, is that of the evidence we will present on the issue of whether the conflict between the HVO and the BH army, was it a civil war or was it an international armed conflict as that term is used in international law. The issue here is not whether there were HV troops, that is, troops of the Republic of Croatia, the army of the Republic of Croatia, in Prozor or Gornji Vakuf or even in the Lasva Valley, although the evidence will show that there were no HV units in the Lasva or Kiseljak Valleys at all relevant times. The issue we will address in our case is whether unity of identity existed between the HV and the HVO; namely, did the HV exercise effective military control over the HVO? That is the test. The evidence will answer that question with a resounding "No." Croatia was a steadfast supporter of the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Croatia was the first country to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent nation. Indeed, it was critical for Croatia that the newly formed borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina be accepted and respected. Were those borders to become subject to negotiations as a result of war activity, Croatia, with substantial territory at the time occupied by the Serbs, would itself have been in greater jeopardy of never regaining its own territory. In other words, if international borders were up for grabs, Croatia was in a very bad situation with 40 or 50 per cent of its own territory occupied by Serbia and the JNA. Croatia was an ally of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war against the Serbs. Serb attacks on Croatia were staged from Bosnia, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Croatian troops did venture into Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend against Serb aggression. The strategy of the Bosnian Serbs was simple: to encircle Central Bosnia in a pincer move, if you will, that would run all the way to the Dalmatian coast and cut off supply routes from which Central Bosnia could receive materiel and aid, and indeed they attempted to do this in 1992. If we could have Map A on the video, please? The army of the Republic of Croatia did enter Bosnia, and as the Court can see from the map -- if we could stay with "A," please, Map A? As Map A depicts, had the JNA and Bosnian Serb militia, which were located again in the pink or purple areas -- if the Court will focus on the large, dark blue area in Herzegovina, below the light green area of Central Bosnia which is marked in small ABiH, if that area of Herzegovina had fallen and had been encircled; in other words - and I'm drawing with the pen - if the JNA and Bosnian Serb militia had been able to complete their move to the coast and to cut Bosnia-Herzegovina at that point, Central Bosnia, all of Central Bosnia, would have been entirely encircled, and without re-supply, it would have collapsed. All munitions and materiel that went to the BH army and the HVO passed through that window, the window I have indicated with the large arrow from the Adriatic Sea, pointing through Dalmatia and into Herzegovina. So the HV, the army of the Republic of Croatia, they did enter Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what did they do? Where I'm drawing dark black lines, they blocked the JNA and Bosnian Serb advance and they kept that window open. They saved Central Bosnia as a result. Croatia also trained and equipped troops to fight in the BH army. Entire units of Muslim refugees who came to Croatia were trained and equipped in Croatia and then went to Bosnia-Herzegovina where they fought as part of the BH army against the JNA and the Bosnian Serb militia. I will now conclude my remarks. I spoke earlier of the orders Tihomir Blaskic issued after he learned, on approximately the 22nd of April, that a massacre had occurred in Ahmici. One of these orders addressed the issue of command and control directly. If I could have the next slide, please? Again, there is a French translation in hard copy, Mr. President. In this order on the 24th of April, Tihomir Blaskic made the following extraordinary assessment, and I quote: "After an assessment carried out in the field, it is apparent that the lower commanders and their units are acting outside the chain of command. They are not executing orders from superiors and are independently making decisions contrary to the received orders. They plan and execute their own combat activities, exert pressure on civilians, and disrupt the work of UNPROFOR, the International Red Cross, and ECMM, which has negative consequences for the HVO and those soldiers who execute the received tasks consistently .... I ORDER: 3. The individuals and groups who are completely out of control are to be arrested immediately and warrants are to be delivered to the commander of the Military Police unit. 4. You are in charge of preventing, with all available means and with the use of force, the most extreme individual and groups who are out of control and who are not protecting civilians, who are demolishing and setting fire to civilian facilities and whose activities are nothing but terrorism." Tihomir Blaskic issued this order to HVO units on the 24th of April, 1993. But he was not sophisticated in media relations or diplomatic relations. He addressed issues of command and control internally and confidentially within the HVO. He didn't lobby BRITBAT, he didn't lobby the European Monitors, he didn't show them orders such as these. The British battalion responded to these events and to a lack of information such as this, lack of response such as the order of the 24th of April, with suspicion, frustration, and even anger, and the Court has seen that here in the courtroom. The Defence does not fault those members of BRITBAT for those views. We simply will point out in our case that had Tihomir Blaskic been more sophisticated at dealing with these entities, query if he would be here today. The Nuremberg War Crimes Tribunal in The High Command Case described the parameters of command responsibility at page 76 of volume 12 of The High Command case, and I quote briefly: "Criminal acts committed by [subordinates] Cannot, in themselves, be charged to a commander on the theory of subordination ... There must be a personal dereliction that can occur only where the act is directly traceable to him or where his failure to properly supervise his subordinates constitutes criminal negligence on his part. In the latter case, it must be a personal neglect amounting to a wanton, immoral disregard of the action of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence. Any other interpretation of International Law would go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law as known to civilised nations." I have tried, in this opening statement, to describe for you some of the steps that Tihomir Blaskic took. There will be more described to you in our case. He did anything but acquiesce in crimes or criminal conduct by HVO units or soldiers. Under what were the most desperate of military circumstances, he diligently attempted to instill professional standards of conduct in what was, in essence, a peasant militia. You will hear from our witnesses that Tihomir Blaskic was a professional soldier, a man free of ethnic prejudice or hate, a man who tried to protect those who could not protect themselves from the horrors of war. At the same time, he is not a forceful person, and he may have been the wrong man for the command that he was given. If that is true, that is not a crime. He did his best. He is not guilty of the charges the Prosecutor has brought against him and the totality of the evidence will so demonstrate. That concludes my opening statement, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. We are going to take a break after this lengthy opening statement. I would like to ask you if you intend to file this with the Court. Is it going to be filed in the two languages of the Tribunal? It has been drafted. Can it be supplied to the Judges as a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: All of the maps and printed quotations that I have referred to will be marked as exhibits, with your leave, Mr. President. The relief model we will also ask be marked as an exhibit. Although it is bulky and heavy and a burden on the court staff, we think it is important that it be an exhibit and remain with the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, you are already asking that the model and the various maps as well as the orders that you have mentioned in your statement be tendered as evidence. Are you asking that this be tendered as evidence today? But I will go back to my original question, the first question today. Are you asking that the model, the maps, and even the other documents that you cited, be tendered as evidence? The second question is: Do you intend to tender your opening statement as evidence to the Judges or do you prefer that this remain in the transcript and that we can then read through the transcript through the interpretation? It seemed to me you had a document. So first question: Are you asking that it be tendered, the model, the maps, and the other documents that you have cited?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The model and maps, Your Honour, I think they should be marked so the record is complete, but there will be witnesses who will come and testify about the maps, about the orders, and I think that's when they should properly be admitted; and even at that time, we can go back, if necessary, and admit the demonstrative aids that I have used in my statements. I did have, Mr. President, a written copy of my opening statement, but I have cut portions out of it and strayed from it from time to time, so I think that it would be most appropriate that we use the transcript as the record of my opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. That's what will be done. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The orders of Colonel Blaskic, you would like to submit them now as exhibits or wait for the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, we won't wait very long, but we would like to wait a few days, and then every order I have referenced in my statement will be presented to Your Honours in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are now going to take a 20- to 25-minute break since Mr. Hayman spoke for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please? Everybody be seated. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Nobilo is going to question the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. Mr. President, Your Honours, the first Defence witness in the case against General Blaskic will provide a historical framework within which the events that are under discussion took place. This historical expert should describe the background to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, and thereby provide a good introduction to an understanding of the war that broke out in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our expert witness will not start with the 6th century, because we consider this to be unnecessary and a waste of time, but we begin his testimony with the creation of nationalist ideas in the former Yugoslavia. He will describe the relationship between the Croats, Serbs, and Muslims in the first Yugoslavia, that is, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. He will describe the relations among those three peoples during the Second World War. He will depict the internal relations in Tito's Yugoslavia, that is, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and he will provide an explanation for the dissolution of Yugoslavia. He will provide the causes of constant conflict among the peoples living in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and he will answer the question why Yugoslavia was the most conflict-ridden state in Europe in the 20th century. Finally, he will provide the findings of his research, which could be summed up as an answer to the question whether, in view of the internal conflicts which Yugoslavia was unable to overcome in the '70s, could it have survived in a democratic system. Your Honours, the expert witness who will be appearing shortly is, in the opinion of many, the best expert on history in the former Yugoslavia. This person represents a part of history himself. He personally knew, talked to, and collaborated with all the relevant political figures in the former Yugoslavia in the last 50 years, ranging from President Josip Tito, with whom he cooperated, to President Franjo Tudjman, with whom he has also cooperated. Our expert is a member of the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences. His name is Professor Dusan Bilandzic, and I would like to now call the witness and ask the usher to bring him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's what we're going to do. Usher, have the witness brought in. I'm not sure I got the name. Dusan Bilandzic; is that correct? Bilandzic, Dusan Bilandzic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Be careful, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing. Please give us your given names, your profession, and then remain standing as long as it takes to read your solemn declaration. After which, you will be seated and answer Mr. Nobilo's questions. Please introduce yourself. You are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My name is Dusan Bilandzic. Currently, I'm retired, but by occupation, a university professor and member of the Academy of Sciences and Arts. I was born --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the time being, that will be sufficient. Please read your solemn declaration which is on the piece of paper which the usher has given to you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have come to testify as part of the trial initiated by the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal against the accused present in this courtroom, General Blaskic. You know the procedure that we use here. First, Mr. Nobilo is going to ask you some questions, and then you will testify freely and, of course, go to the essential points. Mr. Nobilo, you will, I assume, get to the essential points that you want the witness to testify to. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. On behalf of the Defence, I thank you once again for coming. At the outset, as is customary, will you please introduce yourself to the Court? You were born in 1924 in Croatia, and first you went to a Franciscan secondary school and studied to be a clergyman. What happened later on in your life and career?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is a rather long career. After the Franciscan school, which I did not graduate from, I switched to a state gymnasium or secondary school, and from 1938 to 1941, I studied there. In 1941, I joined the partisan movement. I took part in the uprising of 1941, and from 1941 until 1945, I took part in the war and was wounded four times. After the war, I stayed on in the Yugoslav People's Army for 15 years with the rank of colonel and professor of high military schools, at which I taught the history of warfare, with particular reference to the Second World War and the partisan war in Yugoslavia. In 1960, I left the Yugoslav People's Army and started to study social processes and, in the first place, the internal social system of Yugoslavia, the political, economic, and legal systems. Gradually, my studies focused on the most recent period of history, so that in 1967, I became the director of a historical institute in Zagreb. From then on, I focused mostly on research into contemporary history and contemporary social systems, while, at the same time, as a kind of volunteer, I was very active in the political life of Croatia and Yugoslavia. I was a kind of consultant to the highest echelons of the Yugoslav Communist Party as an expert on political processes, and I was a member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Croatia. I took part in the reform of the Yugoslav political system from the beginning of the '60s until the collapse of Yugoslavia. After that, on behalf of the Croatian opposition, I was appointed vice-president of the Republic of Croatia, a position I held for seven months only, but after that, this position was abolished by the collective leadership of the former state. This was the beginning of 1991, and I held that position until the new year. Since then, I have been writing books. I have published a history of Yugoslavia from its foundation, that is, in 1918 until 1986. I have published a book entitled "Yugoslavia after Tito," and today I'm working on a new book which should come out next year and deals with the history from the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire in 1918 until the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1991 and the new balance of forces that was established in Croatia and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you have published eleven books on the history of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in addition to my main field of interest, there are some specific areas, for example, management, the mechanism of management. In Yugoslavia, it has been translated into six languages, including Chinese. Then there's the theory and practise of self-management. If we count all those books, then there are eleven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And more than a hundred articles have been published by you, and you're a member of the Academy of Arts and Sciences, the highest scientific institution in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, you're a member of the most powerful opposition party, the Social Democratic Party of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have no position in the organs of authority?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Would you now go on to your testimony, your presentation. If you have any notes, feel free to use them.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, it is an exceptional honour for me to be able to present here one possible interpretation of the beginning of the crisis, the collapse of the first Yugoslavia, the crisis and break-up of the second Yugoslavia. Of course, this interpretation cannot be, in my personal judgement, absolutely satisfactory because, to date, we do not have a single written history in the form of a synthesis. There are many books, but no real synthesis of this period. Naturally, in my presentation, I cannot, nor should I, as that would be contrary to the principles of science, to be -- I cannot be biased, but if, occasionally, one of my theses may appear to be prejudiced, I ask that this be accepted as something that is unavoidable, but I hope to be able to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let us go back to the period before the formation of the first Yugoslavia. What were the national ideas of the peoples inhabiting the territory of the former Yugoslavia before the end of the First World War, that is, before 1918 and before the foundation of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to make a few observations which I consider to be rather important and which go back a little bit further into history? First of all, history created a community in 1918 which, throughout the period of its existence, had certain permanent characteristics which are essential for an understanding. Unfortunately, I am hearing the French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Press number 6, you will get -- to your right, number 6. You have number 6 to your right, channel number 6.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I should like to avoid listening to any interpretation. Those constant characteristics of Yugoslav society, precisely because they are constant, determined its overall social life, and those were, in the first place, Yugoslavia is a multi-ethnic state in which nations were formed, or at least the three of them, the three more important ones, were formed roughly at the same time when Bismark created Germany or when Garibaldi created Italy but with quite opposing ideologies. Secondly, it is a multi-religious entity, the three large religions: the Catholic, the Orthodox, and Muslim. Fourth (sic), it is a country in which the differences in the level of economic and social development are so vast that they are comparable to the differences between the most developed and least developed European states after the Second World War. Also, various legal systems were inherited from the Austro-Hungarian Empire, from the Ottomans, so that this melting pot was such that in a very small territory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could I ask you to speak a little bit more slowly so that the interpreters can be sure that everything is accurate in the interpretation? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that, Mr. President. I think that, in the world, there is no similar case of such contradictions being in evidence in such a small area. The main contradictions of contemporary civilisations were manifest here in the Balkans, and if those constants are correct - and they are indeed correct - then the problem that arose was: Is it possible for such contradictions which are manifest in such a small area, can they enable or prevent the creation of a sound, normal, stable state? My hypothesis, which is close to a thesis, is that that state put to the test all known social systems. It tested parliamentarianism of the Western type in the first ten years of its existence. That model could not be sustained. Then it tried out dictatorship, a military monarchist dictatorship, which lasted for five or six years. That too collapsed. Then it renewed what remained of parliamentarianism from 1935 until 1941. Then there was a four-year civil war, which is a wealthy treasury regarding behaviour of ethnic groups, political parties -- I'm referring to this four-year war -- and then came a dictatorship modelled on the Stalinist system. It then evolved into a confederation, and even that was not successful. That brings me to the end of my introduction, after which I will answer your question. Let me add that at the same time, with these constant changes that occurred in terms of social system, capitalism, socialism within capitalism, dictatorship on the one hand and the parliamentary system on the other; within Communism, Stalinism on the one hand and anti-Stalinism on the other; centralism and confederalism; and none of these succeeded. Simultaneously with this quest for a social system which would preserve the community, and as those attempts failed, wars broke out in the south Slav areas. Over a period of 100 years, there were six wars, which are also an indicator of the same characteristics; that is, this quest for a system entailed also wars, and these wars were an instrument for finding a solution to the internal contradictions within Yugoslavia, the wars that occurred within the country and around the country. That was what I wanted to say as an introduction prior to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let us go back to the beginning. How come these ethnicities should find themselves in a common state and what ideas did they bring with them to that common state?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: That is precisely the proper question, Your Honours. To make it clear that the Balkans was not the only territory that was packed full with such contradictions which needed to be pacified, I must say that, unfortunately, ever since the French revolution, the ideas of large nation states dominated in Europe. There was Bismark's idea of a Greater Germany, the idea of a Great France, the idea of a Great Russia, the idea of a Great Hungary, a Great Italy, a Great Bulgaria, a Greater Serbia, a Greater Croatia, and even very small national communities of a million or two inhabitants, did not manage to resist this disease of creating a larger nation state. This cost Europe two World Wars which destroyed Europe, making it fall to its knees before others. Suffice it to remind ourselves that two great nations, France and Germany, during a single lifetime, waged three wars: Bismark, Kaiser William, Hitler, and that this made Europe an invalid because nationalist ideologies destroyed the achievements of civilisations which should have served as a foundation for the construction of Europe. I just wish to point out that there were similar situations among the nations of Yugoslavia; namely, the Serb nationalist ideology came into being precisely during the time of the so-called spring of European peoples. That was 1848; that is, the mid 19th century. German ideology at the time, Safarik, Kollar and others, established a theory that all citizens speaking one language, one and the same language, belong to the same nation. According to them, no other criteria was taken into consideration: history, culture, or anything else. A great Serb reformer who has great merit, acknowledged by history, the linguistic reformer Vuk Karadzic, a researcher into the questions of language, found that the Croats, Muslims, Montenegrins, and Serbs speak the same language, and indeed they did speak the same language; the Stokavski, as it was called. About 10 per cent of Croats used a different dialect. The others all spoke the same language. Proceeding from the German linguistic theory, he said, here in the Balkans, from the Austrian borders or, rather, from the Austrian Alps, this entire area of the Balkans, this Slav area, speak either the same language or a similar language, and therefore, they are one nation. What nation are they? "My nation," said he, "the Serbs, they are all Serbs." Responding to the observation that they were Catholics, he said, "Yes, Serbs, but of Catholic religion." What about the Muslims? "Well, they are Serbs of Islamic faith." And that is how this linguistic theory led to a theory that all of them were Serbs from the Alps to Salonika and Constantinople.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, perhaps this would be a good time to pay attention and look at the map that we have on the screen and on the computer screens. Could you please tell us what this map is, how did you come by the map, and who issued the map?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: This is a map which was issued in Belgrade in 1873, and it was used in schools, primary schools, military academies, and other institutions to show, in pictorial form, the Serb people and how they were spread out across the territory according to that linguistic theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, may I come up to the laptop computer to show a new map, and then this map will be clearer to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: On the map, you can see the following: the boundaries of Socialist Yugoslavia, of the Republics of Socialist Yugoslavia. When they are posed on an ethnic map which was issued, as I said, in 1873 in Belgrade, you will be able to see that the Serb nation covers almost all of Croatia, without Zagreb and the Zagroria area; of course, the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Vojvodina, part of Romania, part of Bulgaria, of course Macedonia, right up to Salonika. Jovan Cvijic, the President of the Serb Academy of Science, Professor of the Sorbonne and Member of the French Academy of Science, who was otherwise a very distinguished and renowned, recognised expert, spoke about this state of affairs and said that it was a question of the Slav lack of crystallisation of mass which spread out from Austria to Greece and to Salonika, to Salonika, including Salonika, and even Constantinople, and that there were 9.625.000 inhabitants. The Kingdom of Serbia - the article was written in 1908, during the annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina - at that particular time, Serbia had 2.750.000 inhabitants. So that what Cvijic says were Serbs, in fact, was more than three times a greater number, and this created the conviction on the power and strength of the Serbs. So that is the ethnic criteria. Every nation passes through this phase. It is a phase of nationalism which turns into chauvinism and leads to war. Every nation is to apply another principle in addition to the ethnical principle, at least one, and that is the principle of historic right. "I have the right, as a leader of a nation, to establish borders along those countries who, at some time in history, say a thousand years ago, were within the composition of my one-time ruler." The Serbs had the famous Czar Dusan - I take my name after him; it is my name as well - and Czar Dusan ruled over a large portion of Greece, Albania, Serbia of course, Bulgaria, and so on and so forth, and the Serb Prime Minister, Garasanin, who was a statesman of Serbia, established the right of Serbia to what belonged at one time to the empire of Czar Dusan. So those are the two criteria, and with that, I conclude the Serb ideology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you whether Bosnia and Herzegovina for the most part belonged to the empire of Czar Dusan?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: That is difficult to say. I don't know the precise borders, the frontiers. It is the Middle Ages, and I don't want to enter into the field of the Middle Ages, which is not my field of expertise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us now what nationalist ideas existed with the Croats at the end of the First World War, prior to the formation of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Croatia developed in a quite different manner. The Serb state was born within the Ottoman Empire, and the Ottoman Empire was decadent, it suffered a disease for several hundred years, and therefore, it was a decadent empire, a disintegrating empire, where the legal order was breaking up. Croatia, on the other hand, lived within the composition of the Habsburg monarchy, and the essential difference, the vital difference, lies in the fact that Croatia had, for about 800 years, the status of limited sovereignty. After the disintegration of the Kingdom of Croatia, it entered a personal union with the Kingdom of Hungary, but it retained four elements of sovereignty, and this is exceptionally important in the context of the future Yugoslavia. It retained its name, it was a kingdom, and I shall remind you here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There is a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If there is a mistake -- it must be "Croatia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, they are two kingdoms, two states, Hungary and Croatia, with one king. In Zagreb, there was a viceroy who was called the Ban, and one of these Bans, in a polemics within the Hungarian parliament, the Prime Minister said "Regnum regno non praescribit leges": "Therefore, one kingdom does not have right --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Like Judge Riad, I like to understand everything. There were two states, Hungary and Croatia; is that correct? It was Hungary and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Please make it clear.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: According to an agreement between Hungary and Croatia, a personal union was set up in 1102 which this contract was noted and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me go back to my question. Excuse me. Let me turn to the interpreters. So "Bulgaria" is "Hungary"; is that what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, "Hungary."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Hungary. "Bulgaria" is "Hungary"? Perhaps it's an interpretation question. I thought you were talking about Hungary. Are you talking about Bulgaria? Let me turn to the interpreters here. So "Hungary" is not "Bulgaria." Bulgaria. Bulgaria. All right. Excuse me, interpreters -- I thought that "Hungary" meant "Hungary." So we're talking about Bulgaria and Croatia; that's right? Professor, if you would please speak more -- if you would speak more slowly, that would avoid any errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, quite the contrary. The contract was between Croatia and Hungary, Hungary, which was called Ugarska, Hungary, Hungary, and together they entered into the Austro-Hungarian Empire. So it is Hungary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: There is no physical contiguity between Bulgaria and Croatia, is there? There is a physical contiguity between Croatia and Hungary, so one would expect any arrangements would be between Hungary and Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: So they were two feudal states, and these two feudal states elected a joint king, in this case he was a Hungarian, and this went on until the year 1526 when both those states took on Habsburg as their king, as their sovereign. Croatia retained the status of a kingdom with its borders, with its Sabo or assembly of the Middle Age type, something that could resemble a parliament today, and executive power, led by the Ban, as the viceroy, and it always had a set territory, state territory. So that is the situation with Croatia up until 1918. Now let us look at the nationalist ideology. That was the question. What was it like? What was the Croatian nationalist idea within the composition of the Habsburg monarchy? The Habsburg monarchy had 52 per cent Slavs in its composition and two ruling nations, the Hungarians and the Germans, Austrian Germans, 48 per cent of them. That means that the majority were Slav. With regard to the fact that this was one of the best ordered and civilised, legally most highly developed empires of Europe at the time, it was fairly successful. The Habsburgs were successful in dealing with this complex monarchy. But within the Habsburg monarchy itself, which some called the Danubian monarchy and later on, after 1867, it became known as Austro-Hungary, so within this Habsburg monarchy, nationalist movements began to develop, the Croatian, the Serb, the Hungarian, the German, the Czech, the Polish, the Slovak, the Italian. So these were the national movements that began to emerge. It was a patchwork of nations. Croatia as a kingdom, in the realistic political life, was subjugated to Budapest, under the rule of Budapest, because in Budapest, the joint king reigned, and the real political position of Croatia was in the fact that it was subordinated to Hungary, although it had its own partial sovereignty, restricted sovereignty. There was rivalry between Germany, that is to say, Austria -- let me make one point clear. At that time, the Austrians were part of the German nation and they considered themselves to be Germans and not Austrians. So that is why we sometimes say they are Germans, sometimes Austrians. But, in fact, their national consciousness was that of Germany. They were German, together with Prussia, and they fought with Prussia in deciding which would be the hegemonist to unified Germany. But we won't go into that question at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the Croatian idea and ideals of the day.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just one moment, Mr. President. Counsel Nobilo has asked me a question. I will try to explain that in the briefest terms possible. In view of the fact that in the mid 19th century, or at least the process -- the forming of nations was drawing to a close, the Croatian nation, just like all the other nations in Europe, set itself the overall ideal to create a national state, as was done by Bismark in Germany, by Cavour in Italy, by any other state. However, Croatia at that time made up 5.26 per cent - that is a little over 5 per cent - of the population of the Habsburg monarchy, and it would be an act of suicide, it would be tantamount to a tragedy, an adventuristic undertaking, if Croatia were to follow the road of Serbia. It went in quite a different direction. The leading idea of Croatia, of the spiritual, intellectual elite in Croatia at the time, was that Croatia, by many years of political struggle, should win for itself the status of the third, let us call it, the third unit within the composition of Austro-Hungary. In other words, that Croatia should have the same status that Austria and Hungary hold, and, of course, in that connection, that it be the pivotal point of rallying everybody around and to include Slovenia, Vojvodina, Istria, Dalmatian, and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we now move forward towards the end of World War I and look at the disintegration of Austro-Hungary?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, we won't be able to understand that if I don't add what I am going to say right now, and that is that this concept of Croatia, to be permanently within the composition of Austro-Hungary, came to be called and known as trialism because what existed previously was dualism, and we must know about dualism if we are to explain the subsequent disintegration, and along with that idea, to be permanently within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, there was an openness within the Croatia elite for two other variations. One of these variations and options was with Starcevic at the head of it, and later on the Ustashe would -- the state of Croatia, independent state of Croatia, as a quisling state of Hitler's Germany, would rely on that option. He asked that that be a completely independent state, and he considered that Serbianism was the greatest danger to the Croatian people. Another faction, the third variation or option or concept, was a pro-Yugoslav concept. That is to say, Croatia, at certain points, would agree, together with Serbia, Montenegro, Slovenia, to undertake the formation of a joint Yugoslav state, state of Yugoslavia, as a federation or a confederation. So those were the three basic trends in Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, may we now briefly look at the end of the Second World War and the emergence of the First World, and the emergence of the SHS, the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, how did they come to be together at the end of World War I?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Let me just add, before I go into an important fact, that the First World War lasted for four years and three months. Perhaps the European nations would have gone on fighting for five more years, had it not been for President Wilson who sent several million American soldiers who, in 1918, disembarked in Europe to stop the war and the mutual annihilation of the nations of Europe, but that's a long story. What we must bear in mind here is that for four years and three months, the Croats, the Slovenes, the Muslims and, what will be surprising to you, perhaps, the Serbs, and 40 per cent of them, that is, Serbs from the Vojvadina region, Bosnia and Croatia were, for four years and three months, in the war against Serb Montenegro. When you have this phenomena before you, and it is a phenomena which is astounding and which frightens, if nations are called to unite after four years and three months of warfare, of mutual killing, not only to unite, say, in a period of ten years, but to unite the very moment that the bells rang heralding, declaring an end to the war would enter into a new state without any preparation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had in mind the First World War because you said the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The First World War. Now I come to your question. We have, therefore, as far as the formation of Yugoslavia is concerned, to look at it as follows: Serbia, its elite, its government, the monarch had a war goal, a war objective. They had a vision, a project of what they wanted, a very precise one. Serbia had to demand of the allies, Great Britain, France, Italy, and Russia, an expansion of its territory. In view of the theory of ethnic kinship, this expansion of Serbia had to move towards Bosnia, Vojvodina, Croatia, Dalmacija, the expansion, I'm talking about. But as up until 1918 in the spring, the powers of the entente did not have it in their plan to break up Austro-Hungary. In the Habsberg monarchy, a small state of Croatia remained within the composition of Austro-Hungary. When I say "a small state of Croatia," it is Zagreb, part of Slavonia, but the whole of Bosnia, the greater portion of Dalmacija, a good portion of Slavonia would come under this expanded Serbia. In that vein, the London Treaty was signed between the governments of Serbia, Great Britain, France, and Russia. It was called the Secret London Treaty on the Creation of a Greater Serbia. Russia suggested to Serbia that it avoid joining the whole of Croatia into this new state, this expanded Serbia, because it would have problems because the Croats are Catholics. What happened was the following: Serbia, with the Treaty of London, gained the right to expand towards the west. Croatia, at that time, wished to retain Austro-Hungary, that is, to help retain the Austro-Hungarian Empire, to preserve it, because of the idea of trialism. However, as the possibility was seen of the downfall of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, another solution had to be sought. In 1918, the Croats on the 20th of October broke all state ties with the Habsberg monarchy. They proclaimed Croatia a state, an independent. They proclaimed their autonomy and independence. And we arrive at the phenomena that you mentioned, and that is the 40-day phenomena, the events of the 40 days. Guided by the idea on trialism, that is to say, a state of the south Slavs, a south Slav nation within the composition of the Habsberg monarchy, the representatives of four future federal units, of Tito's federal units, formed a state in Zagreb. The composition was Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Dalmacija, and Vojvodina. The hegemon was Croatia, of course.
