Being the strongest in all respects, demographically, culturally, politically, it became the hegemon. But that state was to retain the governments in Slovenia, Vojvodina, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Dalmacija and was built up as a federation. Simultaneously, a portion of Croatia's politicians who, in the first days of the war in 1914, emigrated to the west, first of all, to Italy and then to France and Great Britain, formed a board, a group of intellectuals which proclaimed themselves the Yugoslav Council for the Creation of Yugoslavia. They wanted a Yugoslavia as a federation or a confederation of nations, and this state created in Zagreb at the end of October 1918, which I mentioned a moment ago, got the name of the state of the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs. After the breakdown of Austro-Hungary, we, therefore, had three states. Everything is very complicated. You have the Kingdom of Serbia, a state, the Kingdom of Montenegro, also a state. In Zagreb, you have the state which was known as the SHS, the state of the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs. So three states there. Of course, Macedonia was not mentioned. That was a case that had been resolved. Now what happened was the following: There were negotiations between Belgrade and Zagreb or, to be more precise, between the national council, which was what the new parliament appointed in Zagreb was called, composed of delegates from Slovenia, Vojvodina, Dalmacija, Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was the national council, and it negotiated with Serbia and Montenegro as to the type of relationships they would be establishing, what kind of state they would be forming. Under pressure, and it would take me a long time to explain all of this, but the Serb prime minister, the famous politician Nikola Pasic, on the 9th of November, 1918 signed a declaration. It was called the Geneva Declaration. It was signed in Geneva. Those two states, that is to say, Serbia on the one side, a kingdom which annexed Montenegro -- there was no longer any Montenegro now. It was annexed. At the beginning of November, I don't remember the date exactly, but its dynasty was abolished by the Serb government, and it did not allow King Nikola, who was the reigning king, Nikola Petrovic, to return to Montenegro. He remained in Italy. Now you have only Serbia, a kingdom, the Kingdom of Serbia, and you have a state in Croatia, and the negotiation were to begin. The Geneva Declaration recognised the status quo, that is to say, that you have two states. We're going to create a sort of confederation. We are going to have the most necessary departments of a joint state, the army, foreign affairs, and so on. Those were the two major departments. As I say, this happened on November the 9th. At the same time, according to the logics of the Treaty of London, which was still in force, the Italian army entered Dalmacija, Istria, and Slovenia to implement the Treaty of London. Simultaneously with that, the Serb army, together with the French army, in expelling the Austrian army, which was moved towards Vojvodina, Bosnia, Croatia, Slovenia, Dalmacija, and Istria, on the one hand, to stop the Italians from moving further inwards and, on the other hand, as this new state that was formed from the states of Austro-Hungary, had no army or police or an apparatus, an administrative apparatus, whereas there were rebellions throughout the country of the Bolshevik type. That is to say, the peasants set fire to the palaces and looted the warehouses of clothing and footwear. There was general panic in Zagreb that the Bolshevik revolution had come to Croatia. In order for the feudal lords to save themselves from this, on the one hand, and to prevent Italy from penetrating further, it sent a delegation to Belgrade and, on the 1st of December, 1918, signed the creation of a unitarian, not a federal, but a unitarian centralist Yugoslavia as a country of an expanded Serbia. So let me add in closing this section --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have arrived at the formation of the first Yugoslavia, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. As we have reached that point, Mr. President, I would like to suggest that we break for lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Usher, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to ask the usher to have our witness brought in. (The witness entered).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. All right. Dr. Bilandzic, did you have a bit of a rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nobilo, the floor is yours to continue to ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go directly to the purpose, to your objective. Don't let the witness stray too far from the objective. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, we have come to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and we won't talk about the history of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, but you will only dwell on a few points. In your introduction, you said that the formation of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia meant also the introduction of parliamentarianism, but it was not successful, so could you explain to the Court why the parliamentary system did not function in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and how that parliamentary era, a kind of democratic era, came to an end in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the first few years after the formation of Yugoslavia, the country was put to the test to see whether it could develop as a parliamentary country. I must pay tribute to the government of Serbia also which introduced the parliamentary system. It was limited in scope, but it was a parliamentary system. However, a fatal mistake was made; namely, proceeding from an ideology which expresses Vrbis claimed that this was a state of a single people, that there weren't any other peoples but just one people, the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes; and proceeding from this premise, all the historical entities were abolished; that is, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Vojvodina, Dalmatia, even Serbia and Montenegro in the administrative sense of the word. Instead of that, the country was administratively divided up into 33 regions with a centralised system of government. The Croats and, to a certain extent, the Slovenes, reacted to this by a large-scale nationalist movement demanding the restoration of historical entities; actually, a return to the Geneva declaration, also requiring that the negotiations that were actually interrupted in Geneva should be resumed. Serbia's reply was: One people cannot negotiate with itself because there is only one single entity; in fact, an expanded Serbia. What occurred was a very severe political parliamentary struggle which gained in intensity. There were rallies, there was a struggle through the mass media or, rather, the newspapers, various organisations were formed to carry on the struggle, and, when this heated debate came to a climax, the regime in Belgrade killed in parliament a group of leaders of Croatia headed by a charismatic leader, Stjepan Radic, whereby the parliamentary system was actually defeated. King Alexander was faced with a dilemma as to what to do next. The killing of three leading Croatian politicians in the parliamentary benches, and two others who were injured, was a very significant political act, and the question was: What should be done with Yugoslavia? But let me go back to your question, why parliamentarianism failed. I think there are several reasons: First, the economic strength in the newly created state was greater in Slovenia and Croatia than in Serbia. Serbia did not have the capabilities, the potential, the results to achieve leadership in the economy, culture, education because it was insufficient in that respect, deficient in that respect. Secondly, demographically too, it could not achieve democracy. Why? The Serbs accounted for about 36 to 38 per cent of the population at the time, and if we assume that, in parliamentary elections, all the Serbs - and that is impossible, but let us go on that assumption - if all the Serbs were to join one political party and achieve the highest possible concentration, then they would have only 36 per cent of the votes, 36 per cent deputy seats in parliament, which means that they would not have a majority. Since the concept behind Yugoslavia was a Greater Serb concept, it could not accept parliamentarianism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, how did King Aleksandar try to save that Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: King Aleksandar, together with the Crown counsel, had two alternatives for a resolution of the Yugoslav crisis. The first alternative was to break up Yugoslavia, to give up on the idea of a Yugoslavia. Then the question arose: If Yugoslavia needs to be disbanded, and it did because it could no longer survive, what should be done? His idea was to amputate the whole of Slovenia, because there was no territorial link between Serbia and Slovenia, and amputate a part of Croatia. Here on the map we can see that the line of the amputation went in such a way that almost the whole of Dalmatia would be attached to Serbia as well as the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a large part of Slavonia and Baranja, so that the Kingdom of Serbia would be expanded and the old concept of a Greater Serbia would become reality. However, the Croats and the Slovenes and, I must add, the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, or, rather, their leaders, opposed the cutting off of Croatia, as did the big powers of the Versailles system. Why did the superpowers suggest to the King or advise the King not to do this? According to the Versailles system, one of the reasons why Yugoslavia was formed in 1918 was that it had two functions: First, to serve as a country that would stand in the way of the possible renewal of German imperialism, Drang nach Osten, because Yugoslavia's geopolitical position was such that if Germany wanted to spread to the east, it had to cover Yugoslavia; and the other function that Yugoslavia had at the time was that, together with a group of countries, the Baltic states, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary -- Hungary less so -- to be a kind of cordon sanitaire against the export of Bolshevism and the Soviet revolution. This amputation proved to be impossible and he adopted a second alternative, the alternative of a dictatorship. He set up a government of generals, headed by General Petar ^ Dzerkovic, who was the commander of his guards, and he believed that the melting pot would, after all, succeed. That is, that the Yugoslav idea would, after all, prevail, and that it needed to be imposed by force. So he again divided Yugoslavia up into nine banovinas or counties in such a way that not one of those counties had the characteristics of an historical entity but were merely administrative units. Counting on the fact that the future would prove him right, he would save Yugoslavia, and gradually he would manage, with the help of the International Community, to preserve and develop it on the basis of the idea of Yugoslavianism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, how did that dictatorship end?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: King Aleksandar was killed in Marseilles in October 1934.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: This problem remains unresolved. It was done by Croatian emigres, the Ustashes and Macedonian émigrés, but an important research of the German Reich, an historian, Eduard Calic, who wrote three volumes on Hitler and Germany, claims that it was the New Germany that was behind this because Hitler came into power in 1933 and the assassination was the work of ultra-rightist forces, pro-Ustashe and pro-Macedonian, extremist Macedonian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the killing of King Aleksandar in Marseilles, what was being done in Yugoslavia? What efforts were made to save it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Let me make one more remark regarding the dictatorship. Regardless of the fact that the King was killed, murdered, it became clear that a dictatorship could not be maintained for long because again the Communists or the Communist Party, in my opinion, came forward with the wrong thesis, claiming that it was a fascist dictatorship headed by a monarch. However, fascist dictatorships, based on the principle of one nation, one party, one Fuehrer could not succeed in Yugoslavia because it was a multi-ethnic state and it simply lost its force, its strength. Not only were the Slovenes and Croats against it but the bourgeois parties in Serbia were against the dictatorship, and it fell. So that in 1935, parliamentarianism was renewed, a kind of Balkan-type parliamentary system with bribes, corruption, fraud, election fraud, et cetera, and second elections were held in 1938, parliamentary elections; but, in fact, those elections enabled an anti-centralist movement, a federalist movement, so that a situation set in of a stalemate, because the forces with the regime and the forces in the opposition were almost in balance. The new Croatian leader, Mrgic, in 1938 won 97 per cent of the votes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can it be said very roughly that the three peoples that we are talking about, because we are discussing here an event that occurred in Bosnia, that is, the Croats, Muslims, and Serbs, formed ranks behind their nationalist leaders as they did in those days?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I must say that these nationalist concentrations were more intense as the years passed. Why? Because the national question became the crucial political question and because the non-Serbs were opposed to centralism and, naturally, they all -- not all of them but most of them -- sided with nationalist parties. The regime, resorting to various means, managed to win over the pro-unitary factors in Croatia, Dalmatia, Slovenia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the fact remains that the grouping was mainly based on nationalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The regime in Belgrade tried to save Yugoslavia once more, eight days before the beginning of the war in Yugoslavia, in Europe, that is, I'm referring to the Second World War, it tried to resolve the Croatian national question by offering the Croatian leader, Mrgic, the formation of a Croatian banovina or county. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, just two or three words about this. In the meantime, Austria was annexed, Czechoslovakia was run over, and it was clear that this was the prelude to the Second World War. On the 1st of September, 1939, Germany attacked Poland. The West, Great Britain, France, America to some extent, wanted to stabilise Yugoslavia as a country which would join the coalition against Hitler, and they exerted pressure on the Belgrade regime to deal with the problem of Yugoslavia in such a way as to make major concessions to the Croats because, in size, they were the second largest people in Yugoslavia. Negotiations were conducted between the Croatian leader Mrgic on the one hand and the leader of the bourgeoise parties, there were several in Serbia at the time, but they couldn't agree on anything. Then the monarch intervened -- not the King, but Prince Paul, who acted as the monarch, on behalf of the monarch -- and he ordered the government - he was a regent and as a regent he was able to do so - he ordered the government to come to an agreement with the Croats, and that agreement was reached eight days before the beginning of the Second World War in such a way that Croatia, which had been divided into two banovinas, Primorska and Savaska, and there were parts also in Vrbaska and some other banovinas or counties, was united but the problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina then arose. When the banovina of Croatia was formed, the question that immediately cropped up was what to be done with Bosnia-Herzegovina. The position taken was that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be divided, that Belgrade and Zagreb, or, rather, Serbia and Croatia, should divide Bosnia and Herzegovina up. An agreement was reached, according to which Croatia acquired, to use the terms used in court here, the provinces of Travnik and Mostar, and several local communities in northern Bosnia, in the Savska river valley, including Brcko, Derventa, Odzaci, Orasje. Also, in relation to socialist Yugoslavia, it won Sid in the region of Srijem. So that was their division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, did this save Yugoslavia, and were the Croats satisfied with this concession? And when Germany attacked, was proper resistance put up or did Yugoslavia fall apart when Germany and Italy attacked?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that that state was already undermined from within, on the one hand, and, on the other, the ruling class in the country was aware of the fact that it was weak, that it lacked power, and so with the assistance of the Croats and the Slovenes, it accepted Hitler's demand for Yugoslavia to join the Tri-partite pact signed on the 25th of March, 1941 in the hope that it will manage to survive without a war, because Hitler did not ask Yugoslavia to participate in its war campaigns. However, a group of generals in Belgrade, encouraged by Great Britain and the United States, carried out a coup d'etat, dismissed the government, and Hitler responded by declaring war. Having broken up Yugoslavia which, in view of its historical regions, was relatively easy to do, Hitler rewarded the Croats by creating a puppet, pro-fascist state, which introduced racial laws with the aim of, one day, making it an ethnically pure state. Srijem was annexed to Croatia, the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that the ethnic structure of the NDH, Independent State of Croatia, was such that, as a state, it was untenable. Why? Out of the 6.300.000 inhabitants of that state, 50 per cent were Serbs and Muslims, not quite 50 per cent. To be more precise, there were about 3.300.000 Croats, and the other two peoples and other minorities accounted for three million. So a state in which the nationalist tension was high could not have survived. However, irrespective of that, in the long run, the Croats would have been punished because they would have shared the destiny of the Slavs, and one day, they would have melted in with other Slav peoples under the heading of Germany. Because it is well-known that Hitler's design was to create a thousand-year-long Neue Ordnung, a new order, according to which the fate of the Croats was sealed. Slovenia was divided into two entities, one of which was proclaimed an integral part of the Third Reich. The other half was next to Italy. Most of Vojvodina was attached to Hungary. Serbia was occupied. Macedonia was attached to Bulgaria; Kosovo to Albania. And Montenegro was to have been a puppet state of Italy's. Similarly, Croatia became a satellite of Berlin and Rome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you will agree with me that fascist Italy annexed the best parts of Croatia, that is, Dalmacija, Istria, and the islands. In that situation, in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which we are particularly interested in, a quisling entity was set up, the independent state of Croatia. Can you tell us what the response was of the people in Croatia and Bosnia who did not except the Ustashe regime? Was there any other movement in Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid the answer to that question is a little more complex. I will come back to that a little later to say that Dalmacija, almost 100 per cent, the people of Dalmacija joined the Partisan Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear it up for the benefit of their Honours. Dalmacija is the coastal part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: But we come to a far more serious question. As Yugoslavia was broken up and segmented, as I have just explained, a new historical situation was created. The internal forces within Yugoslavia, the monarchy, the Serbian bourgeois parties, the Croatian parties, in the first place, the Croatian's peasant party, in view of this, the question that arose was what should be done and how during the occupation? The second question, and it was a much more important question, that is, how the Second World War would end and how they should prepare for the situation that would ensue after the end of the Second World War and for renewing Yugoslavia then. It should be noted that the big powers of the anti-fascist coalition decided that all the lands which Hitler had destroyed and broken up had to be renewed, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and so on. In that respect, Yugoslavia's renewal was secured, regardless of what would happen during the Second World War. But in the interests of understanding the situation, two projects of the future Yugoslavia are essential, because the quisling entities would fall when the Wehrmacht fell. That was clear. But the question then was who would then rule Yugoslavia? There were two visions. One was the Greater Serbia vision and the other was a communist vision. The Communist Party of Yugoslavia organised an insurrection in Yugoslavia. In 1941, it had about 80.000 men under arms; in '42, 150.000; and in 1943, about 300.000 combatants. So that in addition to the eastern front with the Red Army, this was the only front until Italy landed, the Italian forces landed. The Greater Serbian forces felt that Yugoslavia was destroyed by the Croats, and that is why they had to be punished. That is one point. The other, Serbia must correct a disastrous error made, according to the authors of this project, and that was that it had missed its chance to define the western borders of Serbia. Because unless the Second World War was taken advantage of to define those western borders of Serbia, in that case, we would, again, melt into some kind of an undefined Yugoslavia, impersonal Yugoslavia. The Communist Party, after the capitulation of Yugoslavia, set in motion a national all-Serb movement which, in the first few days, had been designed to wage a struggle against the occupiers, to wage a liberation war. But at the end of the war, it was designed to achieve a Greater Serbia, according to this map, on which we see that Croatia virtually no longer exists; Slovenia acquires Trieste, Istria, Fume, Rijeka, a part of the Croatian coast. It is being rewarded. Serbia gained Vojvodina, Montenegro, Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Dalmacija. And being an allied state, it counted on getting from Hungary, Bajo and Pec, this yellow triangle that you can see, a bit of Bulgaria, a bit of Romania. So that would mean the transformation into reality of the Greater Serb project.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Serb nationalist movement was liberated to begin with. Can we name it as the Chetniks, and can you tell us what it turned into?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: They called themselves, at the beginning, the Chetnik Army. Later on, in order to achieve political legitimacy, when they grew in size, their leader, Drazan Mihajlovic was accepted as prime minister in London. He was, of course, in the country, and he was promoted from rank of colonel to rank of general. The royal government in London, that is to say, the ruling Serb government, said to the allies that he was waging a war only against the Germans, that is to say, the occupiers, including the Bulgarians and so on. And Drazan Mihajlovic was said to be the Robin Hood of the Balkan mountains in the American press which was fighting the German divisions. And the myth was created in 1941, 1942, and 1943, the myth about Drazan Mihajlovic as the greatest warrior against fascism. However, what did happen in actual fact? I have to add here that the war broke out between the Partisan Army, Tito's army and Mihajlovic's Chetnik army which, I repeat, was called the Yugoslav Army and which incorporated 100.000. The communists started out from the fact that the Kingdom of Yugoslavia had to be broken up, that is, that it was not to be renewed. For that reason, immediately in 1941 on the first day of the uprising, they formed a federal, military, and political structure for waging the war. That means that every future republic had its own central political institutions and bodies, that every republic already in 1941 had its own national partisan armies. That meant that Serbia, should the communists win, would be brought back to within the boundaries, its boundaries, of about -- that is to say, the boundaries which it had up until 1918, that is to say, the beginning of the First World War, up to 1914, in fact. However, the question arises as to how the communists could revive a country which was destroyed so much internally, within itself. How could they revive this? They did something extraordinary. They made a sort of Yugoslavia synthesis, and this synthesis aspired towards giving each people within Yugoslavia the maximum possible and to retain Yugoslavia in the bargain. That meant that, to the Serbs, they guaranteed that they would live in one state which, for the Serbs, was a sine qua non condition, in fact. They promised the Croats a state, not an independent one, but a republic, a state republic within the frameworks of Yugoslavia. That was also true for the Slovenes, the Macedonians, the Montenegrins, and the nations, the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So from the very first day of the uprising, a federal, political, and military structure was set up. Now, the question arises -- let me say here that the Partisan Army, I was, in 1942, the commander of some 200 partisans. I was a young man of 18 at the time, and all of us were aged between 18 and 25. We were all young men and women. There was nobody older in that war. That was the generation. The communists succeeded in doing something that had never been done before, and that is that, as opposed to the NDH, the Chetniks and the others who based their future on myth, on the myths of history and on hatred towards other nations, the communists taught their partisan fighters that there was no history before them and that history was, in fact, a misconception. It was a barbarianism of the capitalist type, and that for that reason, it should be struck from the political vocabulary, everything that is national. That is one point. The second point is the following: As opposed to hatred towards other peoples, the communists taught their partisans that we were all class brothers, and not only must there be no hatred towards other peoples, but they also taught brotherhood and unity amongst the nations. This utopia on the part of the communists began to rule over the majority of that young partisan generation who fanatically laid down their lives. They were tremendously brave fighters. Then a second question arose, that is, how the individual nations accepted this synthesis, how they reacted to it. There are great differences on that particular point with regard to the participation that the nations of Yugoslavia took in the anti-fascist report, which, I repeat, in 1943 had reached the number of 300.000 partisans. Serbia, in 1941, launched an uprising and played the leading role in raising that uprising. This was also done by Montenegro. But after three to four months, the insurrection in Serbia and Montenegro was stifled. On the contrary, the non-Serb people joined the partisans, because they came to realise that this would no longer be the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, Greater Serbia, but that it would come to be a federation. In that way, the Croats, that is, the Croats with the Serbs in Croatia, who had a great share in the partisan war because they were persecuted by the Ustashe regime, and the main commander of the Croatian army had in his units, under his command, from the summer of 1942 until the summer of 1944, that is to say, two years, he had 50 per cent of all the partisans of Yugoslavia under him. That is, in these Croatian units, half of them were there and half of them were made up of all the other nations of Yugoslavia. Bosnia-Herzegovina was also markedly pro-partisan, because the Serbs outside Serbia supported Tito's movement strongly, so that the partisan movement in Serbia would be revised at the final stages of the war. The war ended in such a way, and I'll be as brief as possible here and I'll condense the Second World War in Yugoslavia, in such a way that the communists had an army of 800.000 soldiers in the final operations for the liberation of Yugoslavia in 1944/1945, that they had total power and authority in their hands. They had the party powers, the party police and army, and party rule. It was secret because the Communist Party of Yugoslavia was a conspiratorial party, whereas formal power and authority was in the hands of organisations which led the war. The war for the Serb people, for the Serb nationalist ideology, ended in a catastrophic manner. The army of 1941 was lost in the confrontation with the Wehrmacht. The army was defeated. Drazan Mihajlovic's army was defeated in 1944. Immediately after the war, the monarchy was liquidated, so that Serbia was returned back into the frameworks of the ones it had before the Balkan wars, before Montenegro and Macedonia became republics. So it lost those two regions. The communists were more lenient on two points towards Serbia, that is to say, Kosovo, which the communists promised self-determination, guided by Lenin's thesis, which means the right to link up with Albania. So that decision was refuted and Vojvodina came back within the frameworks of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, on the one hand, in that anti-fascist war and, on the other hand, I think that you will agree with me when I say it was a civil war as well, what were the positions of the Muslims? Who did they side with, because we're speaking about Bosnia-Herzegovina here, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel Nobilo has asked a question, without which we cannot have a whole picture unless we provide an answer. I maintain that in Yugoslavia there were four wars being waged, the liberation war against the occupier, which was led by the communists and the partisans; second, the war between the individual nations of Yugoslavia, in practical terms, the war between Serbia and Croatia or, let me say, a war between a part of the Serbs in the Chetnik movement and all the other nations. Then, and this is important, within each nation, you had a civil war. The Croats, you had the partisans waging wars against the Croat Ustashes. The Serb partisans waged a war against the Serb Chetniks or Chetnik Serbs. The Slovene partisans waged a war against the military units which were fighting for a revival of a bourgeois Yugoslavia. This was a small force, but it existed. So you had four different types of war being waged. But the wave led by the Communists was victorious, and I might say that Stalin helped Tito in such a way that in 1944, in August or the beginning of September, he gave him nine divisions of the Red Army, one motor mechanised corps, four divisions, airborne divisions, and Tito accepted the offer that the second Bulgarian army should enter Serbia, and therefore, the resistance in 1944 was completely broken down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let us return to the Muslims. Where were they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: So the Second World War ended in the fiasco of the idea of Greater Serbia but also the idea of a Greater Croatia with the Ustashes. The partisans were divided into three factions: one was the pro-partisan faction, and they had Muslim brigades. We even had a Czech brigade, a Hungarian brigade, the Sandor Potefi brigade, and the Muslim, the Muslim one, the Hungarian one, some small German units, the Tilman unit, the Ziska Czech unit, and so the Communists were very skilful in using the national burgeoning forces to strengthen their own forces, although, and this is a paradox of history, the Communists were, to a certain extent, anationalist, they were globalists, cosmopolitans, and therefore, they could allow themselves to solve these questions simply. The Muslim practice, tied to the NDH, the other faction, and the third faction, particularly amongst the intellectuals of the day, asked, on several occasions of Hitler, that Bosnia and Herzegovina become an autonomous state under the immediate, under the direct rule or hand of Hitler's Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, and I'll try and summarise, the Muslims, in the political sense, went into three factions: one joined the anti-fascists, the second joined the Ustashes, and the third was, let us call it the Muslim autonomous idea. But in the military sense, they belonged to two military formations: the Ustashes and the partisans. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, not to go on at too great a length, we come to Tito's socialist Yugoslavia. Could you please tell us the ideals upon which that Yugoslavia was built up and how Tito tried to solve the national question, although you've already mentioned that. You said how he placed this question during the liberation -- but when he came to power, how did he solve the national question and what experiments did he introduce to retain Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Tito's policy, or the policy of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, to be more exact, had a drama of its own kind; that is to say, it was triumphant and was heady with this victory and it thought that a new era of civilisation had begun, The era led by the Soviet Union. It said that the West was decadent and that it would disappear as a regime, as a system, as a social order. Yugoslavia copied everything that Stalin, in the institutional sense, had established. It abolished and banned the multi-party system, it abolished private ownership, private property. It established state ownership. It moved towards a policy of industrialisation and electrification, a rapid change of social structures, and blindly followed the policies and politics of the Soviet Union, of the USSR; and in the peaks of power of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, they thought that Yugoslavia would one day enter into the Soviet Union as one of its republics, and you have with that with two members of the politburo: Kardelj, who was, along with Tito, from 1937 to his death, he was always the No. 2 man in Yugoslavia after Tito. As far as the national question is concerned, there was a utopian vision that nations would wither away, and as socialism was being built up, that nations would disappear, would wither away, the withering away of the nations. In view of the war, intra-nationality war in Yugoslavia during the Second World War, and with regard to the mistrust that was created, any expression of national symbols was banned, nationalist songs and so on, and a great deal of care and attention was paid to prevent any one nation or citizen. There were draconian laws to upset intra-nationality relations. This was very severely punished. This system lasted from the confrontation with Stalin in 1948, when the conflict with Stalin came about. We all know Tito's historical "No" stated to Stalin and the struggle against Stalinism, against Stalin, strengthened Tito's regime. Why? Because the bourgeois forces who ruled in the course of World War II thought that Tito would not be able to tackle Stalin and that his regime would perhaps disintegrate and that Yugoslavia would move towards the West. But, as time went by, the ideological consciousness of the Communists changed to such an extent that those people who said that the Soviet Union was a flourishing garden of a new civilisation, in 1952 they stated at the congress that that was the darkest system ever to be encountered in the history of civilisation, and a complete severance, a new ideology started, the ideology of self-management. In this connection, the whole attitude changed, the attitude towards market mechanisms, market mechanisms had to be revived, planning of the Soviet type was abolished, greater autonomy was given to the work organisations, autonomy to the communes, and a radical reduction in the federal government took place, about 100.000 white collar workers were lost in the reforms, the power of the republics was strengthened, and then, along with this wave of anti-Stalinism, the movement emerged for the transition to a multi-party system, and the links between the leading ideologists of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, Milovan Djilas, with Bevan, Bevan with the British Labour Party, with the Socialists and so on and so forth, and Yugoslavia's slow movement towards the West, the West's aid and assistance to Yugoslavia in helping it resist the Soviet aggression, led to a spiritual climate in which Yugoslavia moved towards the Western model, and it said it would establish a model according to Western Europe. Djilas was -- not only Djilas but many other people, stood on the threshold of setting up an opposition party and, for example, Djilas's idea of 37 communes, Kardelj and Slovenia, 35 were in favour of Djilas's concept. The party, although it was a weak, uneducated intelligentsia, accepted the idea. However, the party piques, Tito, Kardelj, Rankovic, and the other leaders, assessed, and I think they were right in doing so, realistically speaking - it is quite another matter because I personally supported Djilas, I was alongside Djilas in 1953 when he started to raise his platform of this multi-party system. However, through later analysis, I became convinced that Tito was right. He liquidated Djilas politically and, at a meeting of the central committee, stressed the Crown thesis that if Yugoslavia was democratised in the direction of a multi-party system, a civil war in Yugoslavia would be unavoidable. Of course, he did not say that there would be a civil war amongst the Communists, but he considered that the defeated anti-Communist forces in the Second World War, that is, the Croatian rightist pro-Ustashe forces and the bourgeois forces as well as the Chetniks of Drazan Mihajlovic, would use this situation to their own ends and overthrow the regime, the regime would not allow itself to be overthrown, and a civil war would be unavoidable so that we could not move towards democracy at that point, Western democracy. A substitute was found in self-management democracy which was a sort of ideological terminology used which meant none other than the democratisation of the party dictatorship, the democratisation of existing dictatorship and not a change of dictatorship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you said that Tito already, at that time, in the 1950s, came to realise that any kind of democratisation in Yugoslavia would necessarily lead to its disintegration. You also said that, through a later analysis, you came to realise this yourself. Was this confirmed by the events that began with the reforms in 1965 and ended with the Croatian Spring in 1971 when they moved towards liberalisation and further decentralisation? Were the trends towards disintegration burgeoning at that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Concerned about the signs of conflict within the Communist party of Yugoslavia, Tito, on the 13th and 14th of March, 1962, convened a kind of summit, a secret meeting, which went on for three days, rallying about 70 people. His introductory statement was, and I quote: "Monitoring the situation, I have come to the conclusion that there is the threat of the disintegration of Yugoslavia. Why did we wage war for four years when our country is beginning to fall apart?" This was 18 years before his death, and 28 or 27 years prior to the actual disintegration of Yugoslavia. What was it that prompted Tito to be such a good prophet of a bad future? One reason was that he wanted to scare the republican leaders, to force them to obedience because otherwise they would lose power. The other was that, indeed, the disintegration of the Communist party of Yugoslavia had begun. The leading Communist, the Communist leader of Serbia, at a meeting, and I consider this as most instructive, said, "I have read a paper by the Secret Police on what the intelligentsia has on its mind as well as our Communist cadres," and I compared this analysis with an analysis of the Secret Police from 1945, and if the vocabulary has changed slightly, it boils down to the same thing, which means, that from within, this disintegration had started, and the Communists were gradually shifting to nationalist positions, and the republics, being formerly states, in fact, according to the constitution and the law, the republics struggled to allow as little funds as possible to go to Belgrade and to get as much as possible from the joint treasury, and the federal government was paralysed; the federal government was unable to meet because of these conflicts. Three years later, Kardelj, that is the No. 2 man in Yugoslavia, said, "Comrades, our vision on the withering away of nations is utopian. Not only are the nations not withering away, in fact, they are strengthening because they are becoming modern industrial nations, and the more modern and the more developed a nation is in the economic, cultural, educational and every other sense, the stronger it becomes. Therefore, our thesis on the withering away of nations should be rejected. We must accept reality." He proposed a project with two principal premises: Yugoslavia can be saved only as a confederation or as a union of sovereign states, and the federal government and the federal institutions must become no more than green tables at which the republics will negotiate, reach agreements, and decide jointly. That was the first premise. The second was, "We are wrong with regard to the market," and again I'm quoting him, because I remember it well, "The market mechanism is the law of survival of human society," and then he went on to say, and I'm not quoting him anymore: Therefore, without respect for market mechanisms, we will fall apart. Therefore, these two things, are market mechanism of the Western type and, number 2, a confederation. But then, Mr. President, you will ask: Why didn't he come forth with a third premise on a multi-party system when he had resigned to accept these two? Answer: It was not possible. Again, there was fear of disintegration of the country and of the Communist authorities losing power. They were powerful and they thought that, in time, they would achieve their goal without a multi-party system. And then a non-party democracy was proclaimed, a self-management democracy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us digress to make things clearer. Could we call your positions of the '50s and '60s as being the positions of a man believing in Yugoslavia and the chances of that state functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I was a member of two commissions because after Kardelj, Rankovic was removed, he was the vice-president of the republic, and, in fact, he had control over the Secret Police, the UDBA, and then the central committee decided -- or, rather, a year before that, that Yugoslavia should adopt the market mechanism, and a commission was formed, of which I was a member, to draft a project of transition from the economic system in force at the time into a new kind of economic system in which the market would be the dominant force. That was the one commission. On the day that Rankovic fell, by decision of the central committee, I became a member of another commission, the task of which was to study the question of the future of the League of Communists, and a year later, we came to the conclusion that the party should be withdrawn from enterprises, that it should become a kind of educational, ideological propaganda organisation without having actual power. Riding on that wave of democratisation of the party and market mechanism on the other hand, nationalist feelings were given vent to, in Croatia -- a nationalist movement came into being in Croatia in favour of a settlement of accounts; in Slovenia as well as in Serbia, a wave of liberalism came to the fore; and I must say that for six years, there wasn't a single case of arrest for any political offences because there was this wave of democracy which overpowered the police and the party, and that democratic wave also tended towards the same goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A multi-party system and disintegrating processes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain why Tito interrupted that democratic wave or what is known as "the Croatian Spring"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Tito was a rare politician, an autocrat but an enlightened autocrat who had been through the Second World War, he was wounded in it, he had seen the killing of the Second World War, he had witnessed the people of Yugoslavia, he understood all those things very, very well, and he came to the conclusion that in Yugoslavia, another conflict was in the offing. Kardelj imbued him with fear by saying that things rather like the Potefi clubs in Hungary were emerging or something like the Czech Spring and that two dangers were threatening: the danger of an internal conflict and the danger of a Soviet intervention, and that is why all processes should be brought to a halt except one, except one. Even the market mechanism should be halted, the process of democratisation, the withering away of the party. Some of the power that had been taken away from it was restored, but there was one thing only that shouldn't be touched, and that was the course of creating a confederation as the safest way of preserving Yugoslavia; and in that context and in line with those policies, the 1974 constitution was promulgated which has very many confederate elements of which I should like to name three: First, the right of veto of each member of the federation which meant, in practice, that an Albanian who later became the president of Yugoslavia could veto any federal decision, even an initiative could be vetoed. Secondly, strict parity, the so-called ethnic key. In Yugoslavia, the differences between the smallest and the largest republic is 16, between Montenegro and Serbia, for instance. But they had an equal number of members in the government, in the state presidency, even ambassadorial posts. This ethnic key was applied throughout in the belief -- this was something that both he and Kardelj were aware of -- that things should be developed towards a confederation; and then later on, if the republics wanted a multi-party system, they would have one. But the most important thing was to prevent an inter-ethnic conflict, and in their view - they were naive in their belief, as history will show - they believed that it could be saved if this confederate system was established. The 1974 constitution was promulgated, the process of liberalisation was halted, and a bureaucratic blow was inflicted or a firm-hand policy was applied which lasted until his death. But it is noteworthy, it was not the federal centre that applied this firm-hand policy, it was the republican centres. They applied this course, and thereby strengthened the powers of the republics against the federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we now come to the beginning of the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps -- it is ten to four. We could perhaps have a break, unless your next question is very brief. If not, we will have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, this is the best time to break because we have just come to a new heading, which I have noted for myself, "The beginning of the end of Yugoslavia." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will suspend the hearing. I remind you, Professor, you have mentioned -- you said you have given three examples but I've only put down two. You said three points, and I only put down two: equality and the ethnic distribution of all post -- I forgot the third. You can remind me when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we come to something that can be called the beginning of the end of Yugoslavia. During Tito's lifetime, a group of Serb politicians tried to gain some important changes from him and a revision of the 1974 constitution. What happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I must explain to the President of this Honourable Court and give him an answer to the question that he put to me regarding confederation and federation. The constitutional definition of the state of Yugoslavia and the constitutional definition of the republics was worded such that the republics were states with the right to secession. And proceeding from such a constitutional definition, it was logical that constitutional provisions should be passed which implemented that concept, and those are the right to veto from the level of initiatives onwards; secondly, not a proportionate, but a parity principle of representation in federal bodies; and third, a special procedure which determined the process of negotiation among the republics and provinces within the federation. Such a constitutional structure met with resistance in Serbia. The leaders in Serbia, two years after the 1974 constitution was adopted, launched an initiative for a minor revision of the constitution along two main lines. First, the things that were overly decentralised should be reduced so that the greater rights should be restored to the federation; secondly, that the autonomy of Serb provinces, that is Kosovo and Vojvodina, should be limited, but Tito rejected this idea in 1976 when he was 85 years old. And, of course, political shrewdness told the initiators of the reform that Tito's days were numbered and that they should wait. He had vast powers, so that no one could halt the process of confederalisation while he was alive, he and Kardelj. And they were quite old at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after Tito's death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: After Tito's death, a serious economic crisis broke out. A 20-billion-dollar debt was incurred. The state of Yugoslavia was no longer able to service those debts. Basic raw materials, especially fuel and oil, could not be imported. This economic crisis, in itself, forced the ruling class in Yugoslavia to come to grips with the problem. Secondly, in 1981, a revolt broke out in Kosovo and, as a result, the Serb question emerged into the front, and the leadership of Serbia renewed its idea of a constitutional revision. As it was not possible to amend the constitution without the agreement of all the republics, including both provinces, a six-year-old tug-of-war started between Serbia and the other republics and provinces, when all the republics and the provinces of Serbia took up a position warfare, if I may call it that. They dug their heels into the constitution, and they completely blocked Serbia's initiative for an amendment or a revision of the constitution. In the meantime, led by the widespread conviction that, as a confederation, Yugoslavia had become an anti-Serb state which does not recognise what is Serbia's by right because of its strength, and in the belief that Serbia was the only one that had been broken up into three states, that is, Serbia proper and two provinces which had the status of federal units; thirdly, that in all the republics, the first signs were emerging of what was then called particularism, separatism. In Slovenia, a liberal movement started to develop. In Croatia, too, there were certain signs, but it was rather passive, on the whole. It just firmly held on to the 1974 constitution. In short, all the republics defended the constitution so that a popular movement started in Serbia against the constitution on the grounds of the premise that the constitution meant the putting into effect of the old idea of the Komintern to break up Yugoslavia. As you know, the Komintern asked the Communist Party of Yugoslavia to break up Yugoslavia, and the leading politicians in those days were Croats and Slovenes, Kardelj, Tito, Bakaric, and others. It was in response to this movement that Milosevic appeared and who set in practice -- said and implemented the principle that he would no longer negotiate an amendment of the constitution with the republics. He said, "I may negotiate, but I must go outside the existing institutions." And a large scale movement developed which enjoyed the absolute support of the Serb Orthodox Church, the Serb Academy of Sciences which, in 1985, drafted the famous memorandum which, in fact, was a project designed to eliminate the decentralisation in Yugoslavia. So that a movement rallying hundreds of thousands of people were held, two of which, one in Belgrade, one in Kosovo, rallied more than a million people. Milosevic said, "Unless we can achieve it otherwise, we will have to resort to force." Milosevic reckoned that he had at least four or five aces in his hand, which were so powerful and so frightening for the other republics. First of all, he had international support, that is of both the west and the east, not support of him as a person, but support of Yugoslavia, which was a pet of the west and the east. So that anyone defending Yugoslavia, in this case, Milosevic, would surely enjoy the support of the whole world until the very end of both the Warsaw treaty countries and the NATO treaty countries. That was the first ace he held. Secondly, "I can count on the Communist Party of Yugoslavia," he thought, the party that had created Yugoslavia and in which the Yugoslav spirit has not died. Thirdly, I have created a popular national movement to deal with the Serb question in Yugoslavia. Fourthly, he thought, "I have the JNA," which had raised to the highest possible level of socialism and Yugoslavia. It was at the top of the pyramid of its beliefs, and that army would defend both socialism and Yugoslavia, and this was confirmed by the army leadership. "Also, I have the Yugoslav capital and the bank of issue." Having that very, very strong hand of cards in his hand and very powerful arguments to support his views, it would be possible to achieve his goals without an armed struggle, because the balance of forces was such that the other republics had much lesser strength and would have to give way. That is how he reckoned. In the meantime, a Copernik-like about-turn took place. The International Community developed in such a way that, in the east, communism fell in 1989. The League of Communists broke up in January 1990. All that remained was the JNA, and the all-Serb national movement. Those two instruments were still in evidence. The others had collapsed. After Milosevic took over power, he continued -- you may not know this. When, in Croatia, the new forces of the HDZ won and when, in Slovenia, the old regime fell, a series of sessions started among the new heads of state or, rather, new heads of republics and provinces in those days. When Milosevic continued with his prior policy of trying to persuade the republics to carry out a reform, while at the same time preparing for other alternatives, in specific terms, for struggle. I could almost end there, because, as far as I know, you will be hearing another testimony that follows on from what I have said. Your Honours, I can say the following: I'm not here to defend anybody's views, because I would be betraying my profession if I did, but I must say that when I reviewed everything, once again, I came to the conclusion that, from the beginning, Yugoslavia was in a crisis and that it eternally lived in a crisis, but that it survived, to a great degree, thanks to the big powers. Because Tito, in 1945, joined the Soviet bloc without any reservations. When he left the Soviet bloc, and as Stalin did not wage war against him, he then sought not to join NATO or the Warsaw Treaty, and he opted for the policy of non-alignment, managing in 1961 to hold the first non-aligned summit, and that was his policy. But regardless of the fact that Yugoslavia was a non-aligned country, it could not emerge from the grips of the Cold War. The tendencies towards a multi-party system, which could have provoked a civil war, would have been an ideal excuse for Soviet intervention. So that he had to hold on to power firmly so that the country would not break up. That is my professional conviction. I have tried to be impartial, and I hope, maybe wrongly, that I have succeeded. Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. If I have understood well, your main conclusion emanating from the research that you have done, not for the needs of this Court, but for your own scientific studies was that Yugoslavia was not a natural entity and it could not survive without dictatorship. Under conditions of democracy, Yugoslavia, as a state, could not survive.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Let me add, that was a clash of ideas, ideas as to what Yugoslavia is. For the majority of the ruling class in Serbia, the rule was, either Yugoslavia over which we shall dominate or no Yugoslavia at all. The state ideas of Croatia, Slovenia and, later on, Macedonia were quite the contrary. Either a federal or confederate Yugoslavia or no Yugoslavia at all. So these are two different approaches to Yugoslavia, Yugoslavianism, two concepts which were contrarily at war with one another. And the end came as the way we know it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Mr. President, we have completed our examination-in-chief. I have several maps here that we have shown you on the monitor. I have one copy of each, but by tomorrow, we will have small copies for the Judges, Your Honours, and the Prosecution. Could the usher please take these maps from me. The Defence is tendering these exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, these maps have been presented by the Defence as evidence. I suppose that you're going to number them. I also suppose there is no objection on the part of the Prosecution to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Once the registrar has given each of these maps a number -- you don't have to do it, of course, right now, Mr. Dubuisson. Now, Professor, you are now going to be asked questions by the Office of the Prosecutor. That is, Mr. Kehoe is going to conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. I haven't had the pleasure to meet you. My name is Greg Kehoe. My colleagues to my right are Mr. Andrew Cayley, and to his right is Mark Harmon. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, welcome.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I sat with interest on the historical level of your recitation, and I'd like to ask you a couple of questions, if I may, concerning some aspects of your testimony. If we can go back, initially, to the question that was asked by my learned friend, Mr. Nobilo, at the end of his direct examination, and that had to do with your ultimate conclusion concerning the survival of Yugoslavia. Tell me if I'm incorrect in this regard, Doctor, please. Your conclusion would appear to be that Yugoslavia could only survive either as a dictatorship or as some type of loose confederation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the fact is, I would ask another question, and that is that there were a lot of actors, political actors on the scene in Yugoslavia, all the republics, the provinces, the International Community and so on and so forth. Had Ante Markovic, the Prime Minister of the day, who had strong support from the United States of America in concrete terms, President Bush, and Baker, and the European community, the International Community did what it could at the time to save Yugoslavia. The idea was, which was accepted by Markovic, that a transition take place into a pluralistic state of the western democracy type, but that the federal set-up should remain. Had Milosevic and the leaders of Serbia taken long-term negotiations as an option, perhaps a solution could have been found. But it, too, one day would have to end in the way that such a state would enter the European Union, which would, once again -- which would bring it peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Doctor, after 1990 and the first free elections in the former Yugoslavia and the setting up of republics, there was a series of meetings between the republics, including President Milosevic, where very vigorous attempts were made to save Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I think that those negotiations were more a ruse than the truthful desire to retain Yugoslavia. In fact, Milosevic wanted to break down Markovic, the Prime Minister, because he thought that Markovic wanted to establish capitalism and break down socialism. Slovenia and Croatia wanted to overthrow Markovic because they considered that he was the pillar of Yugoslavia, which it would be difficult to maintain; and through coordinated action on the part of Serbia, Croatia and Slovenia, he did not succeed in what he set out to do. Therefore, in Yugoslavia, there are still polemics to this day. Polemics have started. Was it possible to avoid the disintegration of Yugoslavia and the war? Well, in science, in the realm of science, not social sciences, but science, we can do the test again, repeat the test and see if something succeeds or not. But in a society, you cannot repeat your experiments, and it is difficult to turn the film back to the pre-war situation, to see whether something could have worked or not. I think that the thesis remains that Milosevic stuck to the course of either having a socialist Yugoslavia or no Yugoslavia at all. That was his key opinion and key stand on political orientation and concept. And he considered that Serbia had really come to a position of inequality and that had to be changed, altered. And the fact that that meant a deterioration for the other republics, I think that a conflict was imminent. And the actors in this Yugoslav drama aspired, either to gain time, or through negotiation to achieve what they wanted, rather than having truthful ideas about Yugoslavia. And the Yugoslav forces were less strong than the anti-Yugoslavia forces in the sense of defending a federate or confederate Yugoslavia. The balance of power was negative for those forces who wished to retain Yugoslavia as a confederate unit, state unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, Doctor, again in one of your last answers in response to questions by my learned friend, that when Milosevic was deciding what to do, he had five aces that he could use -- I should live to see the day when I have five aces. Nevertheless, he had five aces, and I think you called them -- I think one of the ones that you mentioned was he had the nationalistic movement behind him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after these free elections in 1990 and after these meetings, including these six republic meetings during 1991 where the republics were attempting to hold Yugoslavia together, Milosevic was fuelling the nationalistic passions of the Serbs which led to the concept of a Greater Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was this also taking place: The JNA was making entrees into various regions such as the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you are going to have a separate expose on that. I think that the military piques of the JNA, up until the outbreak of the war, the military piques were not decided and they wavered between being an instrument of Serbia straight-away or to attempt to save Yugoslavia in a way that was not able to succeed. Let me remind you of a discussion I had with a group of some 10 to 15 Generals, the top army leadership in Zagreb, General Kolsak, I came to them for talks -- in fact, they were not talks but a ceremonial occasion, and I said, "Comrades Generals, I know that you would like to have socialism, both socialism and Yugoslavia, and I have nothing against you remaining with those goals in mind, but be careful because one man will destroy both, both sacred ideals, and that is Slobodan Milosevic." None of the Generals had anything to say against that. I am not going to attach great importance to this chance meeting with the Generals of the JNA on that particular occasion, but you know that the Generals did try to convince Milosevic not to amputate Slovenia because, allegedly -- and as an historian, I haven't got documents to bear this out -- but it seems to be the widespread opinion, public opinion, that Serbia, before the war, agreed to have Slovenia step down from Yugoslavia and that Serbia would do nothing to prevent Slovenia from leaving Yugoslavia. However, that is outside the realm of history. Without documents, as a historian, I would not venture to give an opinion on that, how far that is true and how far it isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a question of form I would like to ask. When you answer, Professor, I would appreciate your facing the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, bear with me. At the outset of your testimony, you noted that you were giving one possible interpretation to the break-up of Yugoslavia, and I would just like to ask you about some other aspects of possible interpretations as well, okay, if that's okay? Nevertheless, the passions that were being fuelled on a nationalistic level affected Croatia with the formation of the Kninska Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I did not understand your question. In Croatia, it is true that nationalism developed on the basis of the idea of creating a national state and in response to the danger which came from Serbia. That is certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Krajina, Doctor, the Serbs that were in the Kninska Krajina, which is in the Republic of Croatia, rejected the constitution that was voted upon in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The Cazinska Krajina is almost 100 per cent Muslim and not Serb, Cazinska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The part of the Krajina that incorporates Knin, if I'm mispronouncing this.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes. That is true then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during that, the Serbs in around Knin attempted to set up their own state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you wrote a paper along with various other individuals in 1991 called "Croatia - Between War and Independence" where you discussed the creation of that state in conjunction with the rise of Serb nationalism; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to be fair, Doctor, you are not the only author of that, there were several of your colleagues who were also authors of that piece; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I can't quite recall the article you have in mind, but if you tell me the substance of the article, I will be able to say whether it was mine or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. It is a paper that came from the University of Zagreb, it is in English, the document is called "Croatia - Between War and --"

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know it, and that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are the first author in a list of authors.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, in that paper, you concluded that the formation of a state, such as the Serbs in Krajina, within the Republic of Croatia, was an intolerable situation for the Republic of Croatia, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you stated in that paper that "the territorial integrity of the present Republic of Croatia has its historical and political legality and the ethnic structure of its individual parts does not provide any arguments for any kinds of territorial changes at the cost of Croatia." Now, you wrote that in 1991. Do you believe that now, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, disagreements between -- I'm sorry, go ahead. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: We are not dealing here with what I want to be and whether I agree with the process or not, but if an analysis leads to the fact that a movement or a political party wishes to step down, we're talking about the Knin Serbs from the composition of Croatia, then objectively speaking, this leads to war. Let me remind you that this has a long historical background. The Serbs in Knin, especially in the Knin area, Serbs in Croatia, in the partisan war, had, apart from the Knin Serbs, had a lofty role. They were all within the Communist Party and supported it. However, the Serbs in Knin, in 1939, when the well-known banovina of Croatia was formed, asked for secession, the Knin Serbs. Second, when the disintegration of Yugoslavia came about, the Knin Serbs - in fact the Chetniks - asked to be separated from Croatia and attached to Italy. This was in 1941. Furthermore, in 1944, there was an uprising, a revolt against the partisan Croatia. So this is a long-standing tendency, for Serbs in Croatia not to see the possibility of a livelihood outside the protection of Belgrade, and they are ready to lay down their lives in order to retain Yugoslavia. As this process of the disintegration of Yugoslavia was more or less obvious, they counted upon - and they did this in 1990 - some texts were written, they thought they would form their autonomous province which would become part and parcel of Serbia immediately. However, Serbia was not able to take them in or accept a solution of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back, Doctor, to the Serbs in the Krajina. They first announced their unification as a culturally autonomous entity; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thereafter, they brought into the Knin area the formulation and the establishment of the Republic of Serb Krajina, and with that, all of the trappings of a government?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, a state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular situation, according to the paper that you wrote in 1991, was an intolerable situation for the Republic of Croatia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To magnify the problem, Doctor, you discussed, in that paper, the issue of and the participation of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was your opinion, at the writing of this, that the JNA in the Knin area was merely acting as an army for the Serbs and to protect the Serbs and was participating in the ethnic cleansing of Croats from the Krajina area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I would like to remain within the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can bear with me, Mr. President, I am offering -- it was a possible interpretation offered by the witness concerning the decline and fall, and if you bear with me during my cross, I will take this around and complete the circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But what was stated here -- the articles we are talking about were not tendered in evidence. We don't have to really go through an exegesis of what the Professor wrote in all the various articles. Please remain within the scope -- as much as possible at least, remain within the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm just going into another interpretation of events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noted in your article, and I quote: "A problem of ethnic cleansing should be stressed here; that is, firstly, forcing Croats and all other ethnic groups to flee so that only Serbs remain; and secondly, settling Serb colonists in the emptied areas." Do you remember writing that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You concluded that this use of the armed forces to move the Croats out of the Krajina and the subsequent resettlement of those areas by the Serbs was ethnic cleansing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'd have to clarify what we mean, Mr. President, by "ethnic cleansing." If an ethnic group is forced to relocate itself on another area, then I think that this could be qualified as "ethnic cleansing."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I don't disagree with you. I'm just asking you some questions based on what you wrote. I agree with you that it is ethnic cleansing, and I'm simply asking you the questions as an expert, as a man that knows more than I do.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let's turn, if you will, you talked about the -- part of your enviable five aces, you talked about the rise of nationalism that was happening with the Serbs and Milosevic's playing on that rise of nationalism, and I'd like to talk to you now about the nationalistic movement in Croatia. Now, while there was a nationalistic movement in Serbia that Milosevic was fuelling, there was also a large nationalistic movement in Croatia as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were individuals in Croatia at that time that wanted to reform Croatia to make it look like something similar to the banovina plan of 1939, the sporasom of Cvetkovic-Macel in 1939; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what period the Prosecutor has in mind. In Croatia, there did exist the idea of following Macek's concept of a solution of the relationships between Serbia and Croatia on the basis of the division of Bosnia. That idea did exist. However, one must be aware of the fact that at times like that, when war is imminent, in the air, then the actors of that war have a whole spectrum of different ideas and concepts which are unrealistic and rational and irrational alike which are a ruse to trick the enemy, but precise documents have still not come to view, we still don't have them on a concept of that kind and who wished to realise this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bear with me one moment, Doctor. Mr. Dubuisson, may I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 16, please? I'm not sure -- well, Prosecutor's Exhibit 16. I'm not sure if the Defence just had an exhibit up there of the banovina, but we can use theirs as well. It's the same. What we're talking about is the banovina of 1939. I'll gladly use your map or mine. Yeah, that's the one. If we can take Exhibit 16 out and just put it on the ELMO, it would be helpful. Doctor, I realise that's not precisely an exhibit that you saw before today, but I think you will agree with me it's similar to other copies of a banovina plan as various cartographers have etched it out. Doctor, if this is incorrect in any fashion, I'll gladly use the Defence copy. It really don't make a difference.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: This is the map of the banovinas of Croatia, and it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, with the nationalistic movement that was rising in Croatia, there were politicians that wanted a reformation of Croatia so it would absorb much of Bosnia, so it would look like the banovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Both yes and no.
