In fact, Croatian policy, during negotiations up to the downfall of the old regime and after the old regime, it had a clear-cut rigid stand, that the results of the Second World War should not be infringed with regard to the boundaries of the republic. So what the constitution of 1974 confirmed as the results of the Second World War, Croatian policy considered this to be its primary goal, to retain them. Of course, there were some secret negotiations, and if this went further, I, as an historian, would have to have a document on that. But, of course, a lot was written about the subject and spoken about the subject, that an idea of that kind did exist, and we would require documentation from the Vance-Owen Commission, secret talks with the Serb side, with the Kosovo side, and so on. This is a current political problem for which I am not competent because, as a historian, I would have to have documents to bear that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, one of the proponents for a carving up of Bosnia in the early '90s was President Tudjman, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: In formal terms, no, because at the beginning, he insisted on a confederation but respecting all the republics. This was at first. What happened later -- and I repeat -- secret and confidential exchanges of ideas and talks, one should wait for the documents to appear. Nowhere in any Croatian official documents passed by the parliament or any documentation issued by the government or even Tudjman himself, you cannot find anything beyond the view that Croatia cannot agree to a change of the borders of the former republics. That was the official position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, bear with me one moment. If we can go to the first tape, and if I could ask the interpretation section to translate a portion of the English into French and Bosnian/Serbo-Croatian, and the discussions, some of the discussions in any event, are in Bosnian/Serbo-Croatian. This is a tape, Mr. President, called "Dispatches," which was a show that was exhibited in the United Kingdom in January of 1994. There will be two segments, and I'd like to talk about the first segment first. If we can dim the lights and, Doctor, if you can look at the monitor? (Videotape played) PARTIAL VIDEOTAPE TRANSLATION: ... This was never given in the media, the complete truth about this. (Subtitles follow thereafter)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, what you are discussing during that is the secret meetings in Karadjordjevo on the 10th and 11th of March, 1991, between President Milosevic of Serbia and President Tudjman of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to stick to everything that I have said, that these were secret talks, that nothing is known about them, and I would just add that I think that this is a problem with several aspects to it. One of the aspects is, let us call it tactics or rules to avoid, a direct clash between the two largest nations to come to some sort of an agreement, but I never saw any maps on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor did I have any such maps. These talks between the so-called delegations, they were so-called expert groups, transformed themselves into a sharp dialogue or confrontation so that the only topic was whether Croatia or Serbia or both or either of them would agree to the inviolability of the results of the Second World War. That was the crux of those talks. The Serb side did not clearly and emphatically ever say that it would respect the borders of the existing republics, because if they had, the war would not have occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, you attended a meeting, and pardon me if I mispronounce the name of this town, excuse me, Tikves, T-I-K-V-E-S, which is near Osijek, on about the 10th of April of 1991, as part of a Croatian delegation that met with a Serb delegation to examine maps and to determine which part was going to go to Serbia and which part was going to go to Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: No, it is not right. What is right is that meetings were held. I repeat that 95 per cent of the talks centred around the recognition of the 1974 constitution, and the borders formed as a result of the Second World War, as regards maps and any concrete divisions, they did not exist. There were only ethnic maps, which is quite natural that this should be discussed too, but I repeat, there are no other documents, as far as I know. We did not at all discuss a division in the sense of delineating borders between Serbia and Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina because I and my colleagues did not at all believe, and this was before the war, we did not believe in the realism of such a policy, and we thought that we shouldn't enter into it at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may, Doctor, and I can just move to this exhibit, which is -- whatever the next Prosecution Exhibit is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 464 and the other was 463, for the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, just for record-keeping purposes, there is another clip on the same tape. I don't know if we want to give that second clip another number or make it A or B, whichever is easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my presentation, you were able to see that for 150 years, continuously, Bosnia was appropriated, both by the Serbs and by the Croats. I spoke about the Austrian trialism and I omitted to mention that Stjepan Radic said the following. He wrote a book in 1908, a book entitled "Cvijic", in which he said that Bosnia and Herzegovina was the central Serb land. If you look at the map, you will see that Bosnia is west of Serbia and not a central Serb land. He added: It is not an Alsace and Lorraine, between France and Germany. Bosnia and Herzegovina is for Serbia what Podmoskovlje, the Moscow area, is for Russia. And Radic wrote a book, "The Vital Croatian Right to Bosnia-Herzegovina," within the concept of the creation of a third federal or confederate unit within the framework of Austro-Hungary. Ever since then, there has been an idea which has never disappeared, the idea of dividing Bosnia. These ideas existed on both the Serb and the Croatian side. Within that context, it is possible, but I repeat, I have no documents to that effect, and I cannot judge, but as an expert, I cannot express my views on such a document except by saying that in history there was a tendency on the part of both Serbia and Croatia to divide Bosnia up or even to appropriate the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you gave an interview to the periodical Nacional that was published on the 25th of October, 1996, and that article is before you. I direct your attention to the second page of that article on the lower left-hand corner where it begins, and on to the headline, "The Greatest Disagreements." It begins, "Nacional" -- do you see that, Doctor? I don't want to move ahead until you have that. There is a BCS version contained in there. Excuse me, Doctor, this page. That's the page. It begins in the lower left-hand corner, Doctor, with "The Greatest Disagreements." The question from Nacional reads as follows -- and pardon me, Judge, this is an article I have yet to get translated into French. "Nacional: Could you say now who these people were? Answer: The Croatian Generals Fabijan Trgo, Ivan Kukoc. However, the greatest disagreements that Tudjman and I had occurred during the talks on Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the beginning of 1991, following his negotiations with Milosevic, it was agreed that two commissions should meet and discuss the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tudjman then told us that he had made an agreement with Milosevic in principle and that we would have to work on the maps to work out the practical details. On the Serb side, the talks were attended by a member of the Serb academy, Kosta Mihajlovic, Milosevic's Chief of Cabinet, Kupresic, and pardon my pronunciation, Smilja Avramov and the deputy prime minister of Serbia. Three rounds of talks were held lasting ten hours each in Tikves and in Belgrade. However, these talks did not produce any results. One of the members of our delegation, Josip Sentija, resigned considering such talks absurd. I also tried to warn Tudjman that such talks were pointless. I told him that even if they had agreed in principle, it was impossible to implement the agreement, since there were problems with the maps which, in my opinion, could not be resolved. Endless talks ensued on which side some small valley belonged to, whether it was Serb or Croatian, who had the majority in the town. Moreover, they only let us have western Herzegovina. I warned Tudjman that there were three major obstacles to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that only one obstacle was enough for their agreement to fall through. First of all, the problem of deciding on Croatian and Serb areas; second, the problem of what the Muslims would say to everything. Tudjman replied that they would have nothing to say if the Croats and Serbs agreed. I pointed out the third problem, which was not as serious as the first two, but still remained a problem: What will the International Community say to the agreement? Tudjman replied that the world would accept any agreement coming out of this region." Do you remember giving that interview, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that in the next Nacional, it was stated that I denied some of the statements because this was an off-record conversation while we were having a whiskey. So I denied the reference to the generals and some other pieces contained in this article. I think that this is, how shall I put it, intellectual talk among relatively well-known intellectuals who gave themselves the freedom, the license of academics, and that this was no serious discussion. As you know, we gave up the idea and it failed. It was political tactics to delay the war and to gain time. Any day or month gained would justify these kind of tactics. Therefore, until we have official documents from the state, legal documents, all this remains within the limits of guesswork.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have this discussion with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not in this form, and I repeat that the journalist took advantage of much of what was said. It was not an official interview. It was a talk with a group of journalists who gave themselves a lot of freedom in their interpretation of this. Tudjman had a principled position that an agreement needed to be achieved with Serbia, but specifically what should belong to whom, that never came up. This was just speculation, that the ethnic structure of Bosnia was such. You had the Trezin enclave, the Croat majority here, the Serb majority over there, but I repeat, maps did not exist on the division of Bosnia. That is what I claim under all possible oaths.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, President Tudjman wanted to divide Bosnia with President Milosevic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I repeat that Croatia's policy, from the first day, was that the republican borders must not be changed at any cost. Apart from that, there was just debating, arguing, so as to avoid war, so as to reach some sort of an agreement among two relatively large peoples and to avoid a direct conflict between them. And maybe that was the design behind this whole action in connection with the talks over Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: No documents. Without any documents, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. We have understood, Professor. You've said it several times. I think we understood what you said. Would you please move to another question, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Doctor, nobody from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina participated in these discussions in Karadjordjevo between President Milosevic and President Tudjman, and nobody from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina participated in your discussions with the Serbs that took place less than a month after the meeting in Karadjordjevo; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I said, as far as I know, but whether there were talks between Milosevic and Izetbegovic and also between Tudjman and Izetbegovic, I don't know. But I do know, for instance, that in 1991, a delegation of Muslims sponsored by very prominent figures from Bosnia-Herzegovina went to Belgrade to reach a compromise with Belgrade regarding the future position of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that, too, is part of the political struggle containing elements of ploys and tactics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you were there in Tikves and in Belgrade, and nobody from the Bosnian government was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor obviously doesn't like the answer, but Professor Bilandzic has, three or four times, said exactly what he knows about the whole problem. He is just repeating things, and this is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained. It's almost 5.30, in any case. I think we're going to break now, and we will resume tomorrow at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Court has been adjourned. You may not speak once the Court has been adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.29 p.m. to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of September, 1998 at 2.00 p.m. 25
